Learn more here (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/). California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, an anti-tax advocate says Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied. The opposing view: A city councilmember from Sonoma believes Prop. 43 enables minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/), making it harder to fund vital government functions . Guest Commentary written by Susan Shelley Susan Shelley is the vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The November ballot measure Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) would make it harder to raise taxes in California by restoring the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. A “special tax” is one that earmarks the revenue for specific purposes. Ever since voters approved Proposition 13 in 1978 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)), the California Constitution has clearly stated that cities, counties and special districts may impose special taxes “by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district.” If courts had enforced that plain language, Californians today would not be paying billions of dollars in local taxes. This includes sales tax increases such as L.A. County’s 2024 Measure A (https://homeless.lacounty.gov/measure-a/) for homelessness programs, as well as Measure ULA in the city of Los Angeles (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/), a real estate transfer tax on the value of a property worth more than $5 million, which also pays for homelessness programs and affordable housing. Neither of these received the constitutionally required 66.67% of the vote. In San Francisco, courts upheld a June 2018 special tax (http://sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-appeals-court-upholds-S-F-s-commercial-15903302.php) on commercial real estate leases to fund early education and child care, and a November 2018 special tax on the gross receipts of businesses to pay for homelessness programs. Just like Los Angeles, these measures fell short of a two-thirds vote. In 1978, the people of California added the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes to their constitution. When did the constitution become merely advisory? READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/) It began in 2017 with ambiguous language in a California Supreme Court decision, California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (https://cases.justia.com/california/supreme-court/2017-s234148.pdf?ts=1503939675) . The court suggested — without really deciding — that if a tax increase was placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative instead of by a city council or other government body, the constitution didn’t necessarily apply, and a two-thirds vote wasn’t necessarily required. Lower courts used that language to uphold special taxes that received less than a two-thirds vote if they were placed on the ballot by voters signing initiative petitions. But who are these citizens who want to stand outside grocery stores and farmer’s markets with clipboards to raise their own taxes? They’re often the people who will get the money from the tax. The Upland decision has essentially enabled special interest groups (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) to write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves, pay to collect the signatures to get it on the ballot, and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Some of the court rulings on these Upland taxes have even allowed local government officials to work hand-in-glove with special interests (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/the-fiction-of-citizens-tax-initiatives-in-california/) to get tax increases on the ballot as “citizens’ initiatives.” Now the state government is pushing the envelope even further. The governor recently signed Assembly Bill 1923 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1923), requiring the Fresno County Registrar of Voters to place a citizens’ initiative sales tax increase for transportation on the November ballot (https://fresnoland.org/2026/08/06/better-roads/). The state did this over the objections of the Fresno County Board of Supervisors after it lawfully exercised its discretion under the elections code to order a study of the measure, which would have delayed it past the 2026 ballot deadline and placed it on the 2028 ballot. This is no way to run a railroad. There is no “citizens’ initiative tax increase exception” from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up. Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes. Prop. 43 will restore the two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including any tax increases placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative. It’s a constitutional amendment, overriding court precedents that say otherwise. General taxes, such as those that direct the revenue into a city or county general fund to be spent as elected officials decide, would continue to require only a simple majority vote. Some local government officials may believe voters will not approve general taxes, so they would prefer to tell voters the money from a new tax will be spent only on a specific, urgent need. Their problem isn’t the constitution, it’s trust — if voters don’t trust local elected officials to spend tax money on the most important priorities first, a majority may vote ‘no’ on any tax unless they know what it will fund and it’s guaranteed in writing. Those same officials undoubtedly benefit from having a court-created loophole to raise special taxes without the need for a two-thirds vote. The loophole has been growing with every election. Multiple “citizens’ initiative” tax increases are on the November ballot, racing to squeeze through the opening before voters can hammer boards over it. Prop. 43 gives California voters the opportunity to restore what state courts have eroded: a taxpayer protection in the state constitution that requires local special taxes to have the approval of two-thirds of voters to pass. Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments

By Sandra Lowe, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, a city councilmember from Sonoma believes Proposition 43 enables minority rule, making it harder to fund vital government functions. The opposing view: An anti-tax advocate says Prop. 43 solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied.

Guest Commentary written by

Sometimes things that sound simple are not. 

Let’s take Proposition 43. Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments' decisions: majority rule.  

Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority.

Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected.

In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee.

Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. 

If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote.

The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders.

No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent.

Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions.

The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation.  

Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime.

Majority rule is the basis of our democracy and a hallmark of a free society. Let's not go backward.

By The Mercury News/East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/the-mercury-newseast-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 17, 2026 at 4:30 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 19, 2026 at 11:22 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
California voters have twice approved initiatives making it harder to raise local government taxes — only to have the courts erode them.
Proposition 43 would undo the latest judicial meddling by once again restoring a supermajority threshold for passage of special taxes. Voters should approve it.
There are primarily two types of local taxes:
• A general tax can be used for any legitimate government purpose and is often sought to bolster the budget of a cash-strapped agency.
• A special tax is restricted to a specific purpose such as the construction of a government building or the funding of public transit.
It’s the voting rules for the latter that are at issue with Proposition 43.
Whereas general taxes require a simple majority voter approval for passage, special taxes, under Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996, required two-thirds — until 2017.
That’s when the state Supreme Court, in an unrelated case, distinguished between measures (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/02/19/californias-supreme-court-has-thrown-cities-and-citizens-into-chaos-over-local-taxes/) placed on the ballot through initiative signature-gathering drives and those created by local government agencies.
Building on that court-created distinction, subsequent state appellate court rulings created a two-track system for passage of special taxes: Initiative measures require simple majority approval while those created by government agencies require two-thirds approval.

Endorsement: Elect Michael Melillo to San Jose Unified School District Board of Education (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-michael-melillo-to-san-jose-unified-school-district-board-of-education/)
Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)
Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
As a result, initiative special tax measures that had received more than a majority support, but less than two-thirds that had been thought necessary, have passed, including one for Alameda County (https://www.mercurynews.com/2020/03/06/borenstein-fight-over-alameda-county-sales-tax-hike-just-starting/) and one in Oakland (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/10/17/borenstein-california-needs-clarity-on-vote-requirement-for-taxes/).
This is not what voters intended in 1978 or 1996. The route to the ballot should not determine the vote threshold for passage. Proposition 43 would overturn the court rulings and restore the two-thirds requirement for passage of special taxes.
Perverse incentives
Since 2017, we’ve seen the perverse incentives the court rulings have created. Government agencies have started turning to interest groups to qualify special taxes for the ballot.
For example, Measure RTM (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/09/endorsement-no-on-measure-rtm-transit-tax-bart-manufactured-crisis-vta-doesnt-have-one/), the regional transit sales tax measure voters are currently considering, could have been placed on the ballot by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission. But the measure would have then needed two-thirds voter approval. Instead, transit labor unions and contractors helped fund (https://thevoicesf.org/the-insiders-selling-measure-rtm/) an initiative signature drive and the subsequent campaign for the measure.
Similarly, in Oakland, the city last year put out a budget projection specifying the amount of money needed to fix a structural budget deficit and labor unions (https://netfile.com/public/COAK/campaign/filingsByMeasure/214936600-Measure%20E:%20Oakland%20Public%20Safety,%20Cleanliness%20and%20Community%20Accountability%20Act%20of%202026) then qualified a property tax measure for the June ballot (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/12/endorsement-oakland-measure-e-deceitful-tax-plan-broken-promisesn-another-deceitful-oakland-tax-plan-vote-no-on-measure-e/) for roughly that amount. (Amazingly, it failed to even muster majority support as voters recognized the long string of new taxes in recent years (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/06/05/oakland-tax-measure-e-fails/) had not been used for their promised purposes.)
In each case, the only reason backers qualified the measure through the initiative process was to bypass the two-thirds requirement — to bypass the intent of Propositions 13 and 218.
Reform needed
That said, it is past time for California voters to rethink their approach to property and other local taxes.
First, there are the backwards incentives that stemmed from court interpretations of the language Proposition 13 added to the state Constitution: “Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district … .” (emphasis added)
While backers intended “special taxes” to refer to any levies beyond the Proposition 13 limit of 1% of assessed value, the Supreme Court subsequently narrowed that to mean taxes for a specific purpose. That interpretation was cemented with the passage of Proposition 218.
Consequently, we now distinguish between special taxes for specific purposes that require two-thirds approval (unless qualified through an initiative signature-gathering drive) and general taxes, which require a majority vote and can be used for any legitimate government purpose.
It’s backwards: The tax measures with the fewest restrictions are the easiest to pass. That’s why we often see local governments claiming they want money for a specific purpose but placing measures on the ballot that allow any use of the money.
A glaring example this election season is Palo Alto’s Measure J (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-reject-palo-alto-nov-3-measure-j-sales-tax/), placed on the ballot by the City Council there. The measure, a proposed sales tax increase that requires majority support, is purportedly to purchase and upgrade a community center. But the tax would be permanent, and a future council could use the sales tax money for any purpose.
Property tax unfairness
Second, there’s the fundamental unfairness in Proposition 13, which not only set rules for passage of local taxes but, more significantly, governs how we tax property in California. The measure limits how much the assessed value of a property used to calculate the base tax can increase annually. But it then allows for a resetting of the assessed value when a property is sold.
The result is that people in identical houses can pay vastly different property taxes depending on when they bought their homes. It’s effectively a generational transfer of burden to newer homeowners, making the cost of housing greater for recent, including first-time, buyers.
It’s time to redistribute that burden — not to add to the total collected but to apportion it fairly in a revenue-neutral way between all property owners.
Finally, the debate over the rules for passage of local taxes and for rethinking how we tax property should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal. And it should be decided by voters, not by the courts.
In the meantime, Proposition 43 would merely restore the intent of voters who passed the two prior measures. It merits support.

Confused about how to vote on Proposition 43? Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 7:54 AM
Proposition 43 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article316990490.html) is billed as a taxpayer protection measure that would “save” Proposition 13.
In reality, it would make it much harder for citizen groups in California to pass tax increases to help pay for critical services such as fire and police protection, flood control, health care facilities and road maintenance. It would also make it harder to fund libraries, parks and affordable housing programs that local governments simply can’t afford.
Prop. 43 seeks to raise the threshold necessary to pass citizen tax initiatives from a simple majority to a supermajority of 66.7%, which would mean 33.3% of voters would be calling the shots.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 43 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article316990490.html)
This is why the combined editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee (https://www.modbee.com/), Merced Sun-Star, (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/) Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) oppose Prop. 43. We strongly urge a “no” vote.
Prop. 43 would give the minority too much power. It would make it much harder for citizens to take matters into their own hands when governments can’t — or won’t — finance special projects that serve the public interest.
The ability to pass special taxes is especially important now, when wildfires, droughts and extreme weather leave so many communities vulnerable. Rather than waiting for disaster to strike — or depending on Washington or Sacramento for financial help that may never come — local tax measures can provide revenue to prepare for emergencies, whether it means hiring more firefighters, upgrading equipment or clearing flood channels.
What supporters say
Anti-tax groups, such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (https://www.hjta.org/saveprop13_about_initiative/) andReform California (https://www.reformcalifornia.org/campaigns/stop-the-tax-hikes), say Prop. 43 would merely close a legal loophole used too often by special-interest groups to fund pet projects on the backs of taxpayers.
They say that Proposition 13, which was passed by voters in 1978, specifies that cities, counties and special districts can impose taxes earmarked for specific purposes only with the approval of a supermajority of voters.
Yet language in Prop. 13 and in a follow-up measure, Prop. 218, is somewhat ambiguous. It does not specify that citizen tax initiatives require a supermajority to pass. In a series of court rulings, judges found that they do not.
We weren’t convinced by Prop. 43’s backers, and voters should be skeptical, too. Nor should they buy into the notion that plenty of money is available if public officials would only stop wasting it on misplaced priorities.
“We can go through any budget, and I will find the cost savings to eliminate the need for a tax increase on any ballot in the state of California this cycle,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, the head of Reform California, told us.
Never mind that federal and state budget cuts have taken a huge financial toll on local government. Sacramento County, for example, faced a $101 million budget shortfall this year. Atleast half the deficit (https://cue.gcp.misitemgr.com/cue-web/#/main?uri=https://cue.gcp.misitemgr.com/webservice/escenic/container/ac765bdc-7f13-11f1-a011-277da135f0d0&mimetype=x-ece/container&extra=%7B%22package%22:%22ece-auto-gen-845e918b-ec6d-4d33-a61b-298f753a3360%22%7D) was attributed to cuts in the federal budget.
Communities rely on special taxes for basic services
Local governments have made foolish and, in some cases, corrupt spending decisions, and they should be held accountable.
But Prop. 43 ignores the fact that many communities have no other way to finance needed services.
Take the tiny community of Crockett, population 3,000, located in Contra Costa County.
Volunteers with the Crockett Improvement Association assumed responsibility for landscaping and maintenance of public spaces — a job that included picking up litter, trimming bushes and maintaining streetlights. But when the work became too onerous for aging volunteers, the group gathered signatures to put a $50-a-year parcel tax (https://ballotpedia.org/Crockett_Community_Services_District,_California,_Measure_L,_Maintenance_and_Landscaping_Tax_Initiative_(November_2022)) on the ballot. It passed by 62.78%.
That’s impressive support, yet under Prop. 43, the measure would have failed. Then what? Allow trash and weeds and overgrown bushes to encroach on public spaces?
From a practical standpoint, special taxes are the only way some specific needs can be met, and requiring supermajority approval can create hardships — and even dangers — for communities large and small.
A more reasonable threshold — say 55%, which is the margin required to pass school facility bonds — would be a fair compromise to consider in the future.
For now, voters must decide whether to allow a small minority of voters to dictate whether tax measures should pass. We don’t believe they should.

Guest Commentary written by Susan Shelley Susan Shelley is the vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The November ballot measure Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) would make it harder to raise taxes in California by restoring the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. A “special tax” is one that earmarks the revenue for specific purposes. Ever since voters approved Proposition 13 in 1978 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)), the California Constitution has clearly stated that cities, counties and special districts may impose special taxes “by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district.” If courts had enforced that plain language, Californians today would not be paying billions of dollars in local taxes. This includes sales tax increases such as L.A. County’s 2024 Measure A (https://homeless.lacounty.gov/measure-a/) for homelessness programs, as well as Measure ULA in the city of Los Angeles (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/), a real estate transfer tax on the value of a property worth more than $5 million, which also pays for homelessness programs and affordable housing. Neither of these received the constitutionally required 66.67% of the vote. In San Francisco, courts upheld a June 2018 special tax (http://sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-appeals-court-upholds-S-F-s-commercial-15903302.php) on commercial real estate leases to fund early education and child care, and a November 2018 special tax on the gross receipts of businesses to pay for homelessness programs. Just like Los Angeles, these measures fell short of a two-thirds vote. In 1978, the people of California added the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes to their constitution. When did the constitution become merely advisory? READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/) It began in 2017 with ambiguous language in a California Supreme Court decision, California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (https://cases.justia.com/california/supreme-court/2017-s234148.pdf?ts=1503939675) . The court suggested — without really deciding — that if a tax increase was placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative instead of by a city council or other government body, the constitution didn’t necessarily apply, and a two-thirds vote wasn’t necessarily required. Lower courts used that language to uphold special taxes that received less than a two-thirds vote if they were placed on the ballot by voters signing initiative petitions. But who are these citizens who want to stand outside grocery stores and farmer’s markets with clipboards to raise their own taxes? They’re often the people who will get the money from the tax. The Upland decision has essentially enabled special interest groups (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) to write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves, pay to collect the signatures to get it on the ballot, and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Some of the court rulings on these Upland taxes have even allowed local government officials to work hand-in-glove with special interests (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/the-fiction-of-citizens-tax-initiatives-in-california/) to get tax increases on the ballot as “citizens’ initiatives.” Now the state government is pushing the envelope even further. The governor recently signed Assembly Bill 1923 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1923), requiring the Fresno County Registrar of Voters to place a citizens’ initiative sales tax increase for transportation on the November ballot (https://fresnoland.org/2026/08/06/better-roads/). The state did this over the objections of the Fresno County Board of Supervisors after it lawfully exercised its discretion under the elections code to order a study of the measure, which would have delayed it past the 2026 ballot deadline and placed it on the 2028 ballot. This is no way to run a railroad. There is no “citizens’ initiative tax increase exception” from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up. Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes. Prop. 43 will restore the two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including any tax increases placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative. It’s a constitutional amendment, overriding court precedents that say otherwise. General taxes, such as those that direct the revenue into a city or county general fund to be spent as elected officials decide, would continue to require only a simple majority vote. Some local government officials may believe voters will not approve general taxes, so they would prefer to tell voters the money from a new tax will be spent only on a specific, urgent need. Their problem isn’t the constitution, it’s trust — if voters don’t trust local elected officials to spend tax money on the most important priorities first, a majority may vote ‘no’ on any tax unless they know what it will fund and it’s guaranteed in writing. Those same officials undoubtedly benefit from having a court-created loophole to raise special taxes without the need for a two-thirds vote. The loophole has been growing with every election. Multiple “citizens’ initiative” tax increases are on the November ballot, racing to squeeze through the opening before voters can hammer boards over it. Prop. 43 gives California voters the opportunity to restore what state courts have eroded: a taxpayer protection in the state constitution that requires local special taxes to have the approval of two-thirds of voters to pass. How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/) It began in 2017 with ambiguous language in a California Supreme Court decision, California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (https://cases.justia.com/california/supreme-court/2017-s234148.pdf?ts=1503939675) . The court suggested — without really deciding — that if a tax increase was placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative instead of by a city council or other government body, the constitution didn’t necessarily apply, and a two-thirds vote wasn’t necessarily required. Lower courts used that language to uphold special taxes that received less than a two-thirds vote if they were placed on the ballot by voters signing initiative petitions. But who are these citizens who want to stand outside grocery stores and farmer’s markets with clipboards to raise their own taxes? They’re often the people who will get the money from the tax. The Upland decision has essentially enabled special interest groups (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) to write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves, pay to collect the signatures to get it on the ballot, and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Some of the court rulings on these Upland taxes have even allowed local government officials to work hand-in-glove with special interests (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/the-fiction-of-citizens-tax-initiatives-in-california/) to get tax increases on the ballot as “citizens’ initiatives.” Now the state government is pushing the envelope even further. The governor recently signed Assembly Bill 1923 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1923), requiring the Fresno County Registrar of Voters to place a citizens’ initiative sales tax increase for transportation on the November ballot (https://fresnoland.org/2026/08/06/better-roads/). The state did this over the objections of the Fresno County Board of Supervisors after it lawfully exercised its discretion under the elections code to order a study of the measure, which would have delayed it past the 2026 ballot deadline and placed it on the 2028 ballot. This is no way to run a railroad. There is no “citizens’ initiative tax increase exception” from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up. Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes. Prop. 43 will restore the two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including any tax increases placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative. It’s a constitutional amendment, overriding court precedents that say otherwise. General taxes, such as those that direct the revenue into a city or county general fund to be spent as elected officials decide, would continue to require only a simple majority vote. Some local government officials may believe voters will not approve general taxes, so they would prefer to tell voters the money from a new tax will be spent only on a specific, urgent need. Their problem isn’t the constitution, it’s trust — if voters don’t trust local elected officials to spend tax money on the most important priorities first, a majority may vote ‘no’ on any tax unless they know what it will fund and it’s guaranteed in writing. Those same officials undoubtedly benefit from having a court-created loophole to raise special taxes without the need for a two-thirds vote. The loophole has been growing with every election. Multiple “citizens’ initiative” tax increases are on the November ballot, racing to squeeze through the opening before voters can hammer boards over it. Prop. 43 gives California voters the opportunity to restore what state courts have eroded: a taxpayer protection in the state constitution that requires local special taxes to have the approval of two-thirds of voters to pass. Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments

By Sandra Lowe, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, a city councilmember from Sonoma believes Proposition 43 enables minority rule, making it harder to fund vital government functions. The opposing view: An anti-tax advocate says Prop. 43 solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied.

Guest Commentary written by

Sometimes things that sound simple are not. 

Let’s take Proposition 43. Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments' decisions: majority rule.  

Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority.

Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected.

In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee.

Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. 

If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote.

The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders.

No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent.

Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions.

The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation.  

Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime.

Majority rule is the basis of our democracy and a hallmark of a free society. Let's not go backward.

Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments

By Sandra Lowe, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, a city councilmember from Sonoma believes Proposition 43 enables minority rule, making it harder to fund vital government functions. The opposing view: An anti-tax advocate says Prop. 43 solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied.

Guest Commentary written by

Sometimes things that sound simple are not. 

Let’s take Proposition 43. Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments' decisions: majority rule.  

Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority.

Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected.

In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee.

Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. 

If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote.

The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders.

No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent.

Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions.

The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation.  

Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime.

Majority rule is the basis of our democracy and a hallmark of a free society. Let's not go backward.

California voters have twice approved initiatives making it harder to raise local government taxes — only to have the courts erode them.
Proposition 43 would undo the latest judicial meddling by once again restoring a supermajority threshold for passage of special taxes. Voters should approve it.
There are primarily two types of local taxes:
• A general tax can be used for any legitimate government purpose and is often sought to bolster the budget of a cash-strapped agency.
• A special tax is restricted to a specific purpose such as the construction of a government building or the funding of public transit.
It’s the voting rules for the latter that are at issue with Proposition 43.
Whereas general taxes require a simple majority voter approval for passage, special taxes, under Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996, required two-thirds — until 2017.
That’s when the state Supreme Court, in an unrelated case, distinguished between measures (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/02/19/californias-supreme-court-has-thrown-cities-and-citizens-into-chaos-over-local-taxes/) placed on the ballot through initiative signature-gathering drives and those created by local government agencies.
Building on that court-created distinction, subsequent state appellate court rulings created a two-track system for passage of special taxes: Initiative measures require simple majority approval while those created by government agencies require two-thirds approval.

As a result, initiative special tax measures that had received more than a majority support, but less than two-thirds that had been thought necessary, have passed, including one for Alameda County (https://www.mercurynews.com/2020/03/06/borenstein-fight-over-alameda-county-sales-tax-hike-just-starting/) and one in Oakland (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/10/17/borenstein-california-needs-clarity-on-vote-requirement-for-taxes/).
This is not what voters intended in 1978 or 1996. The route to the ballot should not determine the vote threshold for passage. Proposition 43 would overturn the court rulings and restore the two-thirds requirement for passage of special taxes.
Perverse incentives
Since 2017, we’ve seen the perverse incentives the court rulings have created. Government agencies have started turning to interest groups to qualify special taxes for the ballot.
For example, Measure RTM (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/09/endorsement-no-on-measure-rtm-transit-tax-bart-manufactured-crisis-vta-doesnt-have-one/), the regional transit sales tax measure voters are currently considering, could have been placed on the ballot by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission. But the measure would have then needed two-thirds voter approval. Instead, transit labor unions and contractors helped fund (https://thevoicesf.org/the-insiders-selling-measure-rtm/) an initiative signature drive and the subsequent campaign for the measure.
Similarly, in Oakland, the city last year put out a budget projection specifying the amount of money needed to fix a structural budget deficit and labor unions (https://netfile.com/public/COAK/campaign/filingsByMeasure/214936600-Measure%20E:%20Oakland%20Public%20Safety,%20Cleanliness%20and%20Community%20Accountability%20Act%20of%202026) then qualified a property tax measure for the June ballot (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/12/endorsement-oakland-measure-e-deceitful-tax-plan-broken-promisesn-another-deceitful-oakland-tax-plan-vote-no-on-measure-e/) for roughly that amount. (Amazingly, it failed to even muster majority support as voters recognized the long string of new taxes in recent years (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/06/05/oakland-tax-measure-e-fails/) had not been used for their promised purposes.)
In each case, the only reason backers qualified the measure through the initiative process was to bypass the two-thirds requirement — to bypass the intent of Propositions 13 and 218.
Reform needed
That said, it is past time for California voters to rethink their approach to property and other local taxes.
First, there are the backwards incentives that stemmed from court interpretations of the language Proposition 13 added to the state Constitution: “Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district … .” (emphasis added)
While backers intended “special taxes” to refer to any levies beyond the Proposition 13 limit of 1% of assessed value, the Supreme Court subsequently narrowed that to mean taxes for a specific purpose. That interpretation was cemented with the passage of Proposition 218.
Consequently, we now distinguish between special taxes for specific purposes that require two-thirds approval (unless qualified through an initiative signature-gathering drive) and general taxes, which require a majority vote and can be used for any legitimate government purpose.
It’s backwards: The tax measures with the fewest restrictions are the easiest to pass. That’s why we often see local governments claiming they want money for a specific purpose but placing measures on the ballot that allow any use of the money.
A glaring example this election season is Palo Alto’s Measure J (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-reject-palo-alto-nov-3-measure-j-sales-tax/), placed on the ballot by the City Council there. The measure, a proposed sales tax increase that requires majority support, is purportedly to purchase and upgrade a community center. But the tax would be permanent, and a future council could use the sales tax money for any purpose.
Property tax unfairness
Second, there’s the fundamental unfairness in Proposition 13, which not only set rules for passage of local taxes but, more significantly, governs how we tax property in California. The measure limits how much the assessed value of a property used to calculate the base tax can increase annually. But it then allows for a resetting of the assessed value when a property is sold.
The result is that people in identical houses can pay vastly different property taxes depending on when they bought their homes. It’s effectively a generational transfer of burden to newer homeowners, making the cost of housing greater for recent, including first-time, buyers.
It’s time to redistribute that burden — not to add to the total collected but to apportion it fairly in a revenue-neutral way between all property owners.
Finally, the debate over the rules for passage of local taxes and for rethinking how we tax property should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal. And it should be decided by voters, not by the courts.
In the meantime, Proposition 43 would merely restore the intent of voters who passed the two prior measures. It merits support.

California voters have twice approved initiatives making it harder to raise local government taxes — only to have the courts erode them.
Proposition 43 would undo the latest judicial meddling by once again restoring a supermajority threshold for passage of special taxes. Voters should approve it.
There are primarily two types of local taxes:
• A general tax can be used for any legitimate government purpose and is often sought to bolster the budget of a cash-strapped agency.
• A special tax is restricted to a specific purpose such as the construction of a government building or the funding of public transit.
It’s the voting rules for the latter that are at issue with Proposition 43.
Whereas general taxes require a simple majority voter approval for passage, special taxes, under Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996, required two-thirds — until 2017.
That’s when the state Supreme Court, in an unrelated case, distinguished between measures (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/02/19/californias-supreme-court-has-thrown-cities-and-citizens-into-chaos-over-local-taxes/) placed on the ballot through initiative signature-gathering drives and those created by local government agencies.

Property tax unfairness
Second, there’s the fundamental unfairness in Proposition 13, which not only set rules for passage of local taxes but, more significantly, governs how we tax property in California. The measure limits how much the assessed value of a property used to calculate the base tax can increase annually. But it then allows for a resetting of the assessed value when a property is sold.
The result is that people in identical houses can pay vastly different property taxes depending on when they bought their homes. It’s effectively a generational transfer of burden to newer homeowners, making the cost of housing greater for recent, including first-time, buyers.
It’s time to redistribute that burden — not to add to the total collected but to apportion it fairly in a revenue-neutral way between all property owners.
Finally, the debate over the rules for passage of local taxes and for rethinking how we tax property should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal. And it should be decided by voters, not by the courts.
In the meantime, Proposition 43 would merely restore the intent of voters who passed the two prior measures. It merits support.

Confused about how to vote on Proposition 43? Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 7:54 AM
Proposition 43 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article316990490.html) is billed as a taxpayer protection measure that would “save” Proposition 13.
In reality, it would make it much harder for citizen groups in California to pass tax increases to help pay for critical services such as fire and police protection, flood control, health care facilities and road maintenance. It would also make it harder to fund libraries, parks and affordable housing programs that local governments simply can’t afford.
Prop. 43 seeks to raise the threshold necessary to pass citizen tax initiatives from a simple majority to a supermajority of 66.7%, which would mean 33.3% of voters would be calling the shots.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 43 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article316990490.html)
This is why the combined editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee (https://www.modbee.com/), Merced Sun-Star, (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/) Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) oppose Prop. 43. We strongly urge a “no” vote.
Prop. 43 would give the minority too much power. It would make it much harder for citizens to take matters into their own hands when governments can’t — or won’t — finance special projects that serve the public interest.
The ability to pass special taxes is especially important now, when wildfires, droughts and extreme weather leave so many communities vulnerable. Rather than waiting for disaster to strike — or depending on Washington or Sacramento for financial help that may never come — local tax measures can provide revenue to prepare for emergencies, whether it means hiring more firefighters, upgrading equipment or clearing flood channels.
What supporters say
Anti-tax groups, such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (https://www.hjta.org/saveprop13_about_initiative/) andReform California (https://www.reformcalifornia.org/campaigns/stop-the-tax-hikes), say Prop. 43 would merely close a legal loophole used too often by special-interest groups to fund pet projects on the backs of taxpayers.
They say that Proposition 13, which was passed by voters in 1978, specifies that cities, counties and special districts can impose taxes earmarked for specific purposes only with the approval of a supermajority of voters.
Yet language in Prop. 13 and in a follow-up measure, Prop. 218, is somewhat ambiguous. It does not specify that citizen tax initiatives require a supermajority to pass. In a series of court rulings, judges found that they do not.
We weren’t convinced by Prop. 43’s backers, and voters should be skeptical, too. Nor should they buy into the notion that plenty of money is available if public officials would only stop wasting it on misplaced priorities.
“We can go through any budget, and I will find the cost savings to eliminate the need for a tax increase on any ballot in the state of California this cycle,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, the head of Reform California, told us.
Never mind that federal and state budget cuts have taken a huge financial toll on local government. Sacramento County, for example, faced a $101 million budget shortfall this year. Atleast half the deficit (https://cue.gcp.misitemgr.com/cue-web/#/main?uri=https://cue.gcp.misitemgr.com/webservice/escenic/container/ac765bdc-7f13-11f1-a011-277da135f0d0&mimetype=x-ece/container&extra=%7B%22package%22:%22ece-auto-gen-845e918b-ec6d-4d33-a61b-298f753a3360%22%7D) was attributed to cuts in the federal budget.
Communities rely on special taxes for basic services
Local governments have made foolish and, in some cases, corrupt spending decisions, and they should be held accountable.
But Prop. 43 ignores the fact that many communities have no other way to finance needed services.
Take the tiny community of Crockett, population 3,000, located in Contra Costa County.
Volunteers with the Crockett Improvement Association assumed responsibility for landscaping and maintenance of public spaces — a job that included picking up litter, trimming bushes and maintaining streetlights. But when the work became too onerous for aging volunteers, the group gathered signatures to put a $50-a-year parcel tax (https://ballotpedia.org/Crockett_Community_Services_District,_California,_Measure_L,_Maintenance_and_Landscaping_Tax_Initiative_(November_2022)) on the ballot. It passed by 62.78%.
That’s impressive support, yet under Prop. 43, the measure would have failed. Then what? Allow trash and weeds and overgrown bushes to encroach on public spaces?
From a practical standpoint, special taxes are the only way some specific needs can be met, and requiring supermajority approval can create hardships — and even dangers — for communities large and small.
A more reasonable threshold — say 55%, which is the margin required to pass school facility bonds — would be a fair compromise to consider in the future.
For now, voters must decide whether to allow a small minority of voters to dictate whether tax measures should pass. We don’t believe they should.

Confused about how to vote on Proposition 43? Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 7:54 AM
Proposition 43 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article316990490.html) is billed as a taxpayer protection measure that would “save” Proposition 13.
In reality, it would make it much harder for citizen groups in California to pass tax increases to help pay for critical services such as fire and police protection, flood control, health care facilities and road maintenance. It would also make it harder to fund libraries, parks and affordable housing programs that local governments simply can’t afford.
Prop. 43 seeks to raise the threshold necessary to pass citizen tax initiatives from a simple majority to a supermajority of 66.7%, which would mean 33.3% of voters would be calling the shots.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 43 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article316990490.html)
This is why the combined editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee (https://www.modbee.com/), Merced Sun-Star, (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/) Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) oppose Prop. 43. We strongly urge a “no” vote.
Prop. 43 would give the minority too much power. It would make it much harder for citizens to take matters into their own hands when governments can’t — or won’t — finance special projects that serve the public interest.
The ability to pass special taxes is especially important now, when wildfires, droughts and extreme weather leave so many communities vulnerable. Rather than waiting for disaster to strike — or depending on Washington or Sacramento for financial help that may never come — local tax measures can provide revenue to prepare for emergencies, whether it means hiring more firefighters, upgrading equipment or clearing flood channels.
What supporters say
Anti-tax groups, such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (https://www.hjta.org/saveprop13_about_initiative/) andReform California (https://www.reformcalifornia.org/campaigns/stop-the-tax-hikes), say Prop. 43 would merely close a legal loophole used too often by special-interest groups to fund pet projects on the backs of taxpayers.
They say that Proposition 13, which was passed by voters in 1978, specifies that cities, counties and special districts can impose taxes earmarked for specific purposes only with the approval of a supermajority of voters.
Yet language in Prop. 13 and in a follow-up measure, Prop. 218, is somewhat ambiguous. It does not specify that citizen tax initiatives require a supermajority to pass. In a series of court rulings, judges found that they do not.
We weren’t convinced by Prop. 43’s backers, and voters should be skeptical, too. Nor should they buy into the notion that plenty of money is available if public officials would only stop wasting it on misplaced priorities.
“We can go through any budget, and I will find the cost savings to eliminate the need for a tax increase on any ballot in the state of California this cycle,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, the head of Reform California, told us.
Never mind that federal and state budget cuts have taken a huge financial toll on local government. Sacramento County, for example, faced a $101 million budget shortfall this year. Atleast half the deficit (https://cue.gcp.misitemgr.com/cue-web/#/main?uri=https://cue.gcp.misitemgr.com/webservice/escenic/container/ac765bdc-7f13-11f1-a011-277da135f0d0&mimetype=x-ece/container&extra=%7B%22package%22:%22ece-auto-gen-845e918b-ec6d-4d33-a61b-298f753a3360%22%7D) was attributed to cuts in the federal budget.
Communities rely on special taxes for basic services
Local governments have made foolish and, in some cases, corrupt spending decisions, and they should be held accountable.
But Prop. 43 ignores the fact that many communities have no other way to finance needed services.
Take the tiny community of Crockett, population 3,000, located in Contra Costa County.
Volunteers with the Crockett Improvement Association assumed responsibility for landscaping and maintenance of public spaces — a job that included picking up litter, trimming bushes and maintaining streetlights. But when the work became too onerous for aging volunteers, the group gathered signatures to put a $50-a-year parcel tax (https://ballotpedia.org/Crockett_Community_Services_District,_California,_Measure_L,_Maintenance_and_Landscaping_Tax_Initiative_(November_2022)) on the ballot. It passed by 62.78%.
That’s impressive support, yet under Prop. 43, the measure would have failed. Then what? Allow trash and weeds and overgrown bushes to encroach on public spaces?
From a practical standpoint, special taxes are the only way some specific needs can be met, and requiring supermajority approval can create hardships — and even dangers — for communities large and small.
A more reasonable threshold — say 55%, which is the margin required to pass school facility bonds — would be a fair compromise to consider in the future.
For now, voters must decide whether to allow a small minority of voters to dictate whether tax measures should pass. We don’t believe they should.

Learn more here (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/). California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, an anti-tax advocate says Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied. The opposing view: A city councilmember from Sonoma believes Prop. 43 enables minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/), making it harder to fund vital government functions . Guest Commentary written by Susan Shelley Susan Shelley is the vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The November ballot measure Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) would make it harder to raise taxes in California by restoring the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. A “special tax” is one that earmarks the revenue for specific purposes. Ever since voters approved Proposition 13 in 1978 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)), the California Constitution has clearly stated that cities, counties and special districts may impose special taxes “by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district.” If courts had enforced that plain language, Californians today would not be paying billions of dollars in local taxes. This includes sales tax increases such as L.A. County’s 2024 Measure A (https://homeless.lacounty.gov/measure-a/) for homelessness programs, as well as Measure ULA in the city of Los Angeles (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/), a real estate transfer tax on the value of a property worth more than $5 million, which also pays for homelessness programs and affordable housing. Neither of these received the constitutionally required 66.67% of the vote. In San Francisco, courts upheld a June 2018 special tax (http://sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-appeals-court-upholds-S-F-s-commercial-15903302.php) on commercial real estate leases to fund early education and child care, and a November 2018 special tax on the gross receipts of businesses to pay for homelessness programs. Just like Los Angeles, these measures fell short of a two-thirds vote. In 1978, the people of California added the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes to their constitution. When did the constitution become merely advisory? READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/) It began in 2017 with ambiguous language in a California Supreme Court decision, California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (https://cases.justia.com/california/supreme-court/2017-s234148.pdf?ts=1503939675) . The court suggested — without really deciding — that if a tax increase was placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative instead of by a city council or other government body, the constitution didn’t necessarily apply, and a two-thirds vote wasn’t necessarily required. Lower courts used that language to uphold special taxes that received less than a two-thirds vote if they were placed on the ballot by voters signing initiative petitions. But who are these citizens who want to stand outside grocery stores and farmer’s markets with clipboards to raise their own taxes? They’re often the people who will get the money from the tax. The Upland decision has essentially enabled special interest groups (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) to write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves, pay to collect the signatures to get it on the ballot, and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Some of the court rulings on these Upland taxes have even allowed local government officials to work hand-in-glove with special interests (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/the-fiction-of-citizens-tax-initiatives-in-california/) to get tax increases on the ballot as “citizens’ initiatives.” Now the state government is pushing the envelope even further. The governor recently signed Assembly Bill 1923 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1923), requiring the Fresno County Registrar of Voters to place a citizens’ initiative sales tax increase for transportation on the November ballot (https://fresnoland.org/2026/08/06/better-roads/). The state did this over the objections of the Fresno County Board of Supervisors after it lawfully exercised its discretion under the elections code to order a study of the measure, which would have delayed it past the 2026 ballot deadline and placed it on the 2028 ballot. This is no way to run a railroad. There is no “citizens’ initiative tax increase exception” from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up. Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes. Prop. 43 will restore the two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including any tax increases placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative. It’s a constitutional amendment, overriding court precedents that say otherwise. General taxes, such as those that direct the revenue into a city or county general fund to be spent as elected officials decide, would continue to require only a simple majority vote. Some local government officials may believe voters will not approve general taxes, so they would prefer to tell voters the money from a new tax will be spent only on a specific, urgent need. Their problem isn’t the constitution, it’s trust — if voters don’t trust local elected officials to spend tax money on the most important priorities first, a majority may vote ‘no’ on any tax unless they know what it will fund and it’s guaranteed in writing. Those same officials undoubtedly benefit from having a court-created loophole to raise special taxes without the need for a two-thirds vote. The loophole has been growing with every election. Multiple “citizens’ initiative” tax increases are on the November ballot, racing to squeeze through the opening before voters can hammer boards over it. Prop. 43 gives California voters the opportunity to restore what state courts have eroded: a taxpayer protection in the state constitution that requires local special taxes to have the approval of two-thirds of voters to pass. Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments

By Sandra Lowe, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, a city councilmember from Sonoma believes Proposition 43 enables minority rule, making it harder to fund vital government functions. The opposing view: An anti-tax advocate says Prop. 43 solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied.

Guest Commentary written by

Sometimes things that sound simple are not. 

Let’s take Proposition 43. Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments' decisions: majority rule.  

Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority.

Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected.

In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee.

Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. 

If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote.

The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders.

No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent.

Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions.

The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation.  

Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime.

Majority rule is the basis of our democracy and a hallmark of a free society. Let's not go backward.

Endorsement: Back Prop. 43 to restore voter-approved restrictions on local taxes
Californians have already approved these limits twice, only to have courts erode the will of the electorate

By The Mercury News/East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/the-mercury-newseast-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 17, 2026 at 4:30 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 19, 2026 at 11:22 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
California voters have twice approved initiatives making it harder to raise local government taxes — only to have the courts erode them.
Proposition 43 would undo the latest judicial meddling by once again restoring a supermajority threshold for passage of special taxes. Voters should approve it.
There are primarily two types of local taxes:
• A general tax can be used for any legitimate government purpose and is often sought to bolster the budget of a cash-strapped agency.
• A special tax is restricted to a specific purpose such as the construction of a government building or the funding of public transit.
It’s the voting rules for the latter that are at issue with Proposition 43.
Whereas general taxes require a simple majority voter approval for passage, special taxes, under Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996, required two-thirds — until 2017.
That’s when the state Supreme Court, in an unrelated case, distinguished between measures (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/02/19/californias-supreme-court-has-thrown-cities-and-citizens-into-chaos-over-local-taxes/) placed on the ballot through initiative signature-gathering drives and those created by local government agencies.
Building on that court-created distinction, subsequent state appellate court rulings created a two-track system for passage of special taxes: Initiative measures require simple majority approval while those created by government agencies require two-thirds approval.

Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
As a result, initiative special tax measures that had received more than a majority support, but less than two-thirds that had been thought necessary, have passed, including one for Alameda County (https://www.mercurynews.com/2020/03/06/borenstein-fight-over-alameda-county-sales-tax-hike-just-starting/) and one in Oakland (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/10/17/borenstein-california-needs-clarity-on-vote-requirement-for-taxes/).
This is not what voters intended in 1978 or 1996. The route to the ballot should not determine the vote threshold for passage. Proposition 43 would overturn the court rulings and restore the two-thirds requirement for passage of special taxes.
Perverse incentives
Since 2017, we’ve seen the perverse incentives the court rulings have created. Government agencies have started turning to interest groups to qualify special taxes for the ballot.
For example, Measure RTM (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/09/endorsement-no-on-measure-rtm-transit-tax-bart-manufactured-crisis-vta-doesnt-have-one/), the regional transit sales tax measure voters are currently considering, could have been placed on the ballot by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission. But the measure would have then needed two-thirds voter approval. Instead, transit labor unions and contractors helped fund (https://thevoicesf.org/the-insiders-selling-measure-rtm/) an initiative signature drive and the subsequent campaign for the measure.
Similarly, in Oakland, the city last year put out a budget projection specifying the amount of money needed to fix a structural budget deficit and labor unions (https://netfile.com/public/COAK/campaign/filingsByMeasure/214936600-Measure%20E:%20Oakland%20Public%20Safety,%20Cleanliness%20and%20Community%20Accountability%20Act%20of%202026) then qualified a property tax measure for the June ballot (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/12/endorsement-oakland-measure-e-deceitful-tax-plan-broken-promisesn-another-deceitful-oakland-tax-plan-vote-no-on-measure-e/) for roughly that amount. (Amazingly, it failed to even muster majority support as voters recognized the long string of new taxes in recent years (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/06/05/oakland-tax-measure-e-fails/) had not been used for their promised purposes.)
In each case, the only reason backers qualified the measure through the initiative process was to bypass the two-thirds requirement — to bypass the intent of Propositions 13 and 218.
Reform needed
That said, it is past time for California voters to rethink their approach to property and other local taxes.
First, there are the backwards incentives that stemmed from court interpretations of the language Proposition 13 added to the state Constitution: “Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district … .” (emphasis added)
While backers intended “special taxes” to refer to any levies beyond the Proposition 13 limit of 1% of assessed value, the Supreme Court subsequently narrowed that to mean taxes for a specific purpose. That interpretation was cemented with the passage of Proposition 218.
Consequently, we now distinguish between special taxes for specific purposes that require two-thirds approval (unless qualified through an initiative signature-gathering drive) and general taxes, which require a majority vote and can be used for any legitimate government purpose.
It’s backwards: The tax measures with the fewest restrictions are the easiest to pass. That’s why we often see local governments claiming they want money for a specific purpose but placing measures on the ballot that allow any use of the money.
A glaring example this election season is Palo Alto’s Measure J (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-reject-palo-alto-nov-3-measure-j-sales-tax/), placed on the ballot by the City Council there. The measure, a proposed sales tax increase that requires majority support, is purportedly to purchase and upgrade a community center. But the tax would be permanent, and a future council could use the sales tax money for any purpose.
Property tax unfairness
Second, there’s the fundamental unfairness in Proposition 13, which not only set rules for passage of local taxes but, more significantly, governs how we tax property in California. The measure limits how much the assessed value of a property used to calculate the base tax can increase annually. But it then allows for a resetting of the assessed value when a property is sold.
The result is that people in identical houses can pay vastly different property taxes depending on when they bought their homes. It’s effectively a generational transfer of burden to newer homeowners, making the cost of housing greater for recent, including first-time, buyers.
It’s time to redistribute that burden — not to add to the total collected but to apportion it fairly in a revenue-neutral way between all property owners.
Finally, the debate over the rules for passage of local taxes and for rethinking how we tax property should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal. And it should be decided by voters, not by the courts.
In the meantime, Proposition 43 would merely restore the intent of voters who passed the two prior measures. It merits support.
