Confused about how to vote on Proposition 43? Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 7:54 AM
Proposition 43 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article316990490.html) is billed as a taxpayer protection measure that would “save” Proposition 13.
In reality, it would make it much harder for citizen groups in California to pass tax increases to help pay for critical services such as fire and police protection, flood control, health care facilities and road maintenance. It would also make it harder to fund libraries, parks and affordable housing programs that local governments simply can’t afford.
Prop. 43 seeks to raise the threshold necessary to pass citizen tax initiatives from a simple majority to a supermajority of 66.7%, which would mean 33.3% of voters would be calling the shots.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 43 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article316990490.html)
This is why the combined editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee (https://www.modbee.com/), Merced Sun-Star, (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/) Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) oppose Prop. 43. We strongly urge a “no” vote.
Prop. 43 would give the minority too much power. It would make it much harder for citizens to take matters into their own hands when governments can’t — or won’t — finance special projects that serve the public interest.
The ability to pass special taxes is especially important now, when wildfires, droughts and extreme weather leave so many communities vulnerable. Rather than waiting for disaster to strike — or depending on Washington or Sacramento for financial help that may never come — local tax measures can provide revenue to prepare for emergencies, whether it means hiring more firefighters, upgrading equipment or clearing flood channels.
What supporters say
Anti-tax groups, such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (https://www.hjta.org/saveprop13_about_initiative/) andReform California (https://www.reformcalifornia.org/campaigns/stop-the-tax-hikes), say Prop. 43 would merely close a legal loophole used too often by special-interest groups to fund pet projects on the backs of taxpayers.
They say that Proposition 13, which was passed by voters in 1978, specifies that cities, counties and special districts can impose taxes earmarked for specific purposes only with the approval of a supermajority of voters.
Yet language in Prop. 13 and in a follow-up measure, Prop. 218, is somewhat ambiguous. It does not specify that citizen tax initiatives require a supermajority to pass. In a series of court rulings, judges found that they do not.
We weren’t convinced by Prop. 43’s backers, and voters should be skeptical, too. Nor should they buy into the notion that plenty of money is available if public officials would only stop wasting it on misplaced priorities.
“We can go through any budget, and I will find the cost savings to eliminate the need for a tax increase on any ballot in the state of California this cycle,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, the head of Reform California, told us.
Never mind that federal and state budget cuts have taken a huge financial toll on local government. Sacramento County, for example, faced a $101 million budget shortfall this year. Atleast half the deficit (https://cue.gcp.misitemgr.com/cue-web/#/main?uri=https://cue.gcp.misitemgr.com/webservice/escenic/container/ac765bdc-7f13-11f1-a011-277da135f0d0&mimetype=x-ece/container&extra=%7B%22package%22:%22ece-auto-gen-845e918b-ec6d-4d33-a61b-298f753a3360%22%7D) was attributed to cuts in the federal budget.
Communities rely on special taxes for basic services
Local governments have made foolish and, in some cases, corrupt spending decisions, and they should be held accountable.
But Prop. 43 ignores the fact that many communities have no other way to finance needed services.
Take the tiny community of Crockett, population 3,000, located in Contra Costa County.
Volunteers with the Crockett Improvement Association assumed responsibility for landscaping and maintenance of public spaces — a job that included picking up litter, trimming bushes and maintaining streetlights. But when the work became too onerous for aging volunteers, the group gathered signatures to put a $50-a-year parcel tax (https://ballotpedia.org/Crockett_Community_Services_District,_California,_Measure_L,_Maintenance_and_Landscaping_Tax_Initiative_(November_2022)) on the ballot. It passed by 62.78%.
That’s impressive support, yet under Prop. 43, the measure would have failed. Then what? Allow trash and weeds and overgrown bushes to encroach on public spaces?
From a practical standpoint, special taxes are the only way some specific needs can be met, and requiring supermajority approval can create hardships — and even dangers — for communities large and small.
A more reasonable threshold — say 55%, which is the margin required to pass school facility bonds — would be a fair compromise to consider in the future.
For now, voters must decide whether to allow a small minority of voters to dictate whether tax measures should pass. We don’t believe they should.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.

Proposition 43, sponsored by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, may seem pretty basic. It is a constitutional amendment that would restore the two-thirds vote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) requirement to enact all local “special taxes” intended to fund a specific, designated purpose, such as public safety or libraries.
But the ballot measure is more accurately seen as Howard Jarvis giving voters a chance to tell the California Supreme Court to take a hike — to stop sabotaging popular state laws that create obstacles to newer and higher taxes. Just as Republican-appointed U.S. Supreme Court justices tailor their legal rulings to meet broad conservative objectives, some of the state supremes’ most important rulings feel contrived to achieve the goals of the liberal Sacramento establishment.
An obvious example is the court’s contrary rulings on citizen initiatives, which have long since lost their noble patina of being a way for voters to use “direct democracy” to overcome special interests. Instead, as political scientists and journalists have documented for decades, such measures are routinely stage-managed (https://digitalcommons.lmu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=3172&context=llr) by powerful forces — unions, business organizations and, yes, elected officials.
Sometimes the state’s justices choose to ignore this history. Sometimes they emphasize it.
In a 2017 case involving a ballot measure related to cannabis dispensaries in the city of Upland, the court, on a 5-2 vote, drastically changed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) how the judicial system interpreted voter-approved state laws, especially Proposition 13 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)) — the landmark 1978 legislation that kicked off a national taxpayer rights movement. The majority held that since the measure reached the ballot because of a citizen signature-gathering campaign — instead of the direct action of a local government body — simple majority support was necessary for enactment, not the two-thirds vote specified in Proposition 13.
Why? Because, per Justice Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar, courts must “liberally construe the public’s statewide and local initiative power.” Yet it was literally undisputed that the Upland measure reached the ballot not because of a backlash to City Hall machinations from residents but because of a well-funded effort by a cannabis trade group.
But in 2018, the state high court unanimously agreed (https://www.rstreet.org/commentary/public-sector-unions-win-big-at-the-california-supreme-court-in-getting-san-diego-pension-reforms-overturned/) that a 2012 ballot measure approved by a huge majority of San Diegans that ended defined benefit pensions for most new city hires should be invalidated (https://www.rstreet.org/commentary/public-sector-unions-win-big-at-the-california-supreme-court-in-getting-san-diego-pension-reforms-overturned/). Why? Because the fact that 116,000 city residents signed the petitions to put the measure on the ballot was tainted by the strong support of then-Mayor Jerry Sanders, who was depicted as trying to get around laws that require the city to collectively bargain changes in employment terms.
What he was trying to get around was the fact that the City Council majority, allied with unions, bitterly opposed pension changes despite compensation costs eating up a massive and growing chunk of city budgets. As former City Attorney Jan Goldsmith wrote (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2012/02/29/initiative-process-is-first-power-reserved-to-the-people/), “Never in the history of California has there ever been a requirement to negotiate with labor unions over terms of a citizens’ initiative placed on the ballot by voter signatures.”
These rulings can’t be squared. The state Supreme Court treats the citizen initiative process as a sacrosanct part of state government that must be “liberally construed” when it comes to allowing tax hikes on a simple majority vote. But when it comes to a campaign to contain pension costs, it is collective bargaining laws that must be “liberally construed” — not “the public’s statewide and local initiative power.”

Endorsement: Yes on California Proposition 43, make it harder to raise taxes

FILE – In this June 7, 1978 file photo, Paul Gann, left, and Howard Jarvis, right, celebrate as their co-authored tax initiative Proposition 13 takes a commanding lead and ultimately won in the California primary in Los Angeles. (AP Photo/File)
By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: August 9, 2026 at 9:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: August 28, 2026 at 12:16 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
On the California Secretary of State’s website describing qualified statewide measures for the November ballot, voters will see a three-word reference to Proposition 43 referring to “Local taxes: limitation.” (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/qualified-ballot-measures) It’s ironic the initiative that has sparked the most backroom drama in years is depicted with such little fanfare.
Prop. 43 was placed on the ballot by a panicked California Legislature after a last- minute deal was struck with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to pull the association’s more sweeping Local Taxpayer Protection Act from the ballot. Despite the complicated inside-the-Capitol machinations with lobbyists and lawmakers, the resulting measure is rather simple.
If voters approve it, Prop. 43 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/aca-22.pdf) would close a court created loophole that allowed some local special taxes to evade the two-thirds vote requirement — taxes for specific items such as transit, housing, flood control and parks. Specifically, tax increases that are placed on the ballot by citizens via signature-gathering.
This change would restore the threshold to the design of 1978’s tax-limiting Proposition 13. Since then, a series of bone-headed court decisions (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/courts-widen-the-door-to-even-more-local-taxes-in-california/) determined that voters could approve citizen-driven special tax increases by a simple majority, while maintaining the two-thirds rule for special tax increases directly placed on the ballot by local governments. This loophole led to abuses, as unions served as the cat’s paw for local officials by gathering signatures to place tax increases on the ballot and pass them with less than a two-thirds vote.
So, the bottom line: Vote yes on Proposition 43, as it will impede local governments from getting around the two-thirds vote for special taxes to bail themselves out of endless budget debacles. As the economy has stumbled and local governments have burned through “free” COVID money from Washington, D.C., municipalities increasingly are turning to bonds and tax increases (https://caltax.org/2026/03/20/voters-to-decide-fate-of-80-local-tax-and-bond-measures-in-june/) .
Money is fungible. If voters approve “special” (https://flooddistrict.marincounty.gov/question/what-is-a-special-tax/) taxes, that leaves more money in the general fund to spend as usual. That typically means bigger paychecks and pensions for powerful public-employee unions. The two-thirds vote threshold is one of the few ways that California taxpayers can at least try to force their elected officials to live within their means.
That said, we’re disappointed that the final measure doesn’t include a ban and rollback of local transfer taxes. For instance, Los Angeles’ disastrous “mansion tax” (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2025-10-01/apartment-development-pipeline-dries-up-in-spite-of-demand-for-housing) not only imposes astronomical rates on Angelenos who sell pricey homes (currently a 4% tax on homes priced above $5.4 million and 5.5% on those priced above $10.9 million) — but applies to apartment and commercial properties. Predictably, that has quashed housing production in Los Angeles.

The original initiative by HJTA banned real estate transfer taxes above a minor documentary transfer fee. Proponents ultimately pulled that initiative from the ballot at the last minute after the Legislature passed the compromise (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) measure that deals only with the two-thirds vote issue. The Legislature also agreed to pull a separate ballot measure designed to make it harder to pass all future tax-limitation efforts, including this one. This deal to remove the transfer-tax portion of the initiative led to a split within the business coalition that had supported it.
Complicating matters further, the key Democratic lawmakers who placed the current measure on the ballot are calling for voters to reject it. They placed it there simply as a means to derail something that they viewed as far worse (https://sdvoice.info/on-your-november-ballot-proposition-43/) because it protected taxpayers even more from the predations of government and allied special interests. But voters needn’t get caught up in the back story, however interesting as insight into Sacramento’s sausage-making process.
As it stands, the final measure is praiseworthy, as it puts the brakes on local governments’ ability to collude with special interests to more easily raise your taxes. Vote yes on Prop. 43 to make it harder to raise taxes.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.

Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. Proposition 43, sponsored by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, may seem pretty basic. It is a constitutional amendment that would restore the two-thirds vote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) requirement to enact all local “special taxes” intended to fund a specific, designated purpose, such as public safety or libraries.
But the ballot measure is more accurately seen as Howard Jarvis giving voters a chance to tell the California Supreme Court to take a hike — to stop sabotaging popular state laws that create obstacles to newer and higher taxes. Just as Republican-appointed U.S. Supreme Court justices tailor their legal rulings to meet broad conservative objectives, some of the state supremes’ most important rulings feel contrived to achieve the goals of the liberal Sacramento establishment.
An obvious example is the court’s contrary rulings on citizen initiatives, which have long since lost their noble patina of being a way for voters to use “direct democracy” to overcome special interests. Instead, as political scientists and journalists have documented for decades, such measures are routinely stage-managed (https://digitalcommons.lmu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=3172&context=llr) by powerful forces — unions, business organizations and, yes, elected officials.
Sometimes the state’s justices choose to ignore this history. Sometimes they emphasize it.
In a 2017 case involving a ballot measure related to cannabis dispensaries in the city of Upland, the court, on a 5-2 vote, drastically changed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) how the judicial system interpreted voter-approved state laws, especially Proposition 13 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)) — the landmark 1978 legislation that kicked off a national taxpayer rights movement. The majority held that since the measure reached the ballot because of a citizen signature-gathering campaign — instead of the direct action of a local government body — simple majority support was necessary for enactment, not the two-thirds vote specified in Proposition 13.
Why? Because, per Justice Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar, courts must “liberally construe the public’s statewide and local initiative power.” Yet it was literally undisputed that the Upland measure reached the ballot not because of a backlash to City Hall machinations from residents but because of a well-funded effort by a cannabis trade group.

Proposition 43, sponsored by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, may seem pretty basic. It is a constitutional amendment that would restore the two-thirds vote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) requirement to enact all local “special taxes” intended to fund a specific, designated purpose, such as public safety or libraries.
But the ballot measure is more accurately seen as Howard Jarvis giving voters a chance to tell the California Supreme Court to take a hike — to stop sabotaging popular state laws that create obstacles to newer and higher taxes. Just as Republican-appointed U.S. Supreme Court justices tailor their legal rulings to meet broad conservative objectives, some of the state supremes’ most important rulings feel contrived to achieve the goals of the liberal Sacramento establishment.
An obvious example is the court’s contrary rulings on citizen initiatives, which have long since lost their noble patina of being a way for voters to use “direct democracy” to overcome special interests. Instead, as political scientists and journalists have documented for decades, such measures are routinely stage-managed (https://digitalcommons.lmu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=3172&context=llr) by powerful forces — unions, business organizations and, yes, elected officials.
Sometimes the state’s justices choose to ignore this history. Sometimes they emphasize it.
In a 2017 case involving a ballot measure related to cannabis dispensaries in the city of Upland, the court, on a 5-2 vote, drastically changed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) how the judicial system interpreted voter-approved state laws, especially Proposition 13 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)) — the landmark 1978 legislation that kicked off a national taxpayer rights movement. The majority held that since the measure reached the ballot because of a citizen signature-gathering campaign — instead of the direct action of a local government body — simple majority support was necessary for enactment, not the two-thirds vote specified in Proposition 13.
Why? Because, per Justice Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar, courts must “liberally construe the public’s statewide and local initiative power.” Yet it was literally undisputed that the Upland measure reached the ballot not because of a backlash to City Hall machinations from residents but because of a well-funded effort by a cannabis trade group.

Endorsement: Yes on California Proposition 43, make it harder to raise taxes

By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: August 9, 2026 at 9:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: August 28, 2026 at 12:16 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
On the California Secretary of State’s website describing qualified statewide measures for the November ballot, voters will see a three-word reference to Proposition 43 referring to “Local taxes: limitation.” (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/qualified-ballot-measures) It’s ironic the initiative that has sparked the most backroom drama in years is depicted with such little fanfare.
Prop. 43 was placed on the ballot by a panicked California Legislature after a last- minute deal was struck with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to pull the association’s more sweeping Local Taxpayer Protection Act from the ballot. Despite the complicated inside-the-Capitol machinations with lobbyists and lawmakers, the resulting measure is rather simple.
If voters approve it, Prop. 43 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/aca-22.pdf) would close a court created loophole that allowed some local special taxes to evade the two-thirds vote requirement — taxes for specific items such as transit, housing, flood control and parks. Specifically, tax increases that are placed on the ballot by citizens via signature-gathering.
This change would restore the threshold to the design of 1978’s tax-limiting Proposition 13. Since then, a series of bone-headed court decisions (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/courts-widen-the-door-to-even-more-local-taxes-in-california/) determined that voters could approve citizen-driven special tax increases by a simple majority, while maintaining the two-thirds rule for special tax increases directly placed on the ballot by local governments. This loophole led to abuses, as unions served as the cat’s paw for local officials by gathering signatures to place tax increases on the ballot and pass them with less than a two-thirds vote.
So, the bottom line: Vote yes on Proposition 43, as it will impede local governments from getting around the two-thirds vote for special taxes to bail themselves out of endless budget debacles. As the economy has stumbled and local governments have burned through “free” COVID money from Washington, D.C., municipalities increasingly are turning to bonds and tax increases (https://caltax.org/2026/03/20/voters-to-decide-fate-of-80-local-tax-and-bond-measures-in-june/) .
Money is fungible. If voters approve “special” (https://flooddistrict.marincounty.gov/question/what-is-a-special-tax/) taxes, that leaves more money in the general fund to spend as usual. That typically means bigger paychecks and pensions for powerful public-employee unions. The two-thirds vote threshold is one of the few ways that California taxpayers can at least try to force their elected officials to live within their means.
That said, we’re disappointed that the final measure doesn’t include a ban and rollback of local transfer taxes. For instance, Los Angeles’ disastrous “mansion tax” (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2025-10-01/apartment-development-pipeline-dries-up-in-spite-of-demand-for-housing) not only imposes astronomical rates on Angelenos who sell pricey homes (currently a 4% tax on homes priced above $5.4 million and 5.5% on those priced above $10.9 million) — but applies to apartment and commercial properties. Predictably, that has quashed housing production in Los Angeles.

The original initiative by HJTA banned real estate transfer taxes above a minor documentary transfer fee. Proponents ultimately pulled that initiative from the ballot at the last minute after the Legislature passed the compromise (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) measure that deals only with the two-thirds vote issue. The Legislature also agreed to pull a separate ballot measure designed to make it harder to pass all future tax-limitation efforts, including this one. This deal to remove the transfer-tax portion of the initiative led to a split within the business coalition that had supported it.
Complicating matters further, the key Democratic lawmakers who placed the current measure on the ballot are calling for voters to reject it. They placed it there simply as a means to derail something that they viewed as far worse (https://sdvoice.info/on-your-november-ballot-proposition-43/) because it protected taxpayers even more from the predations of government and allied special interests. But voters needn’t get caught up in the back story, however interesting as insight into Sacramento’s sausage-making process.
As it stands, the final measure is praiseworthy, as it puts the brakes on local governments’ ability to collude with special interests to more easily raise your taxes. Vote yes on Prop. 43 to make it harder to raise taxes.

Endorsement: Yes on California Proposition 43, make it harder to raise taxes

FILE – In this June 7, 1978 file photo, Paul Gann, left, and Howard Jarvis, right, celebrate as their co-authored tax initiative Proposition 13 takes a commanding lead and ultimately won in the California primary in Los Angeles. (AP Photo/File)
By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: August 9, 2026 at 9:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: August 28, 2026 at 12:16 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
On the California Secretary of State’s website describing qualified statewide measures for the November ballot, voters will see a three-word reference to Proposition 43 referring to “Local taxes: limitation.” (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/qualified-ballot-measures) It’s ironic the initiative that has sparked the most backroom drama in years is depicted with such little fanfare.
Prop. 43 was placed on the ballot by a panicked California Legislature after a last- minute deal was struck with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to pull the association’s more sweeping Local Taxpayer Protection Act from the ballot. Despite the complicated inside-the-Capitol machinations with lobbyists and lawmakers, the resulting measure is rather simple.
If voters approve it, Prop. 43 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/aca-22.pdf) would close a court created loophole that allowed some local special taxes to evade the two-thirds vote requirement — taxes for specific items such as transit, housing, flood control and parks. Specifically, tax increases that are placed on the ballot by citizens via signature-gathering.
This change would restore the threshold to the design of 1978’s tax-limiting Proposition 13. Since then, a series of bone-headed court decisions (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/courts-widen-the-door-to-even-more-local-taxes-in-california/) determined that voters could approve citizen-driven special tax increases by a simple majority, while maintaining the two-thirds rule for special tax increases directly placed on the ballot by local governments. This loophole led to abuses, as unions served as the cat’s paw for local officials by gathering signatures to place tax increases on the ballot and pass them with less than a two-thirds vote.
So, the bottom line: Vote yes on Proposition 43, as it will impede local governments from getting around the two-thirds vote for special taxes to bail themselves out of endless budget debacles. As the economy has stumbled and local governments have burned through “free” COVID money from Washington, D.C., municipalities increasingly are turning to bonds and tax increases (https://caltax.org/2026/03/20/voters-to-decide-fate-of-80-local-tax-and-bond-measures-in-june/) .
Money is fungible. If voters approve “special” (https://flooddistrict.marincounty.gov/question/what-is-a-special-tax/) taxes, that leaves more money in the general fund to spend as usual. That typically means bigger paychecks and pensions for powerful public-employee unions. The two-thirds vote threshold is one of the few ways that California taxpayers can at least try to force their elected officials to live within their means.
That said, we’re disappointed that the final measure doesn’t include a ban and rollback of local transfer taxes. For instance, Los Angeles’ disastrous “mansion tax” (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2025-10-01/apartment-development-pipeline-dries-up-in-spite-of-demand-for-housing) not only imposes astronomical rates on Angelenos who sell pricey homes (currently a 4% tax on homes priced above $5.4 million and 5.5% on those priced above $10.9 million) — but applies to apartment and commercial properties. Predictably, that has quashed housing production in Los Angeles.

The original initiative by HJTA banned real estate transfer taxes above a minor documentary transfer fee. Proponents ultimately pulled that initiative from the ballot at the last minute after the Legislature passed the compromise (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) measure that deals only with the two-thirds vote issue. The Legislature also agreed to pull a separate ballot measure designed to make it harder to pass all future tax-limitation efforts, including this one. This deal to remove the transfer-tax portion of the initiative led to a split within the business coalition that had supported it.
Complicating matters further, the key Democratic lawmakers who placed the current measure on the ballot are calling for voters to reject it. They placed it there simply as a means to derail something that they viewed as far worse (https://sdvoice.info/on-your-november-ballot-proposition-43/) because it protected taxpayers even more from the predations of government and allied special interests. But voters needn’t get caught up in the back story, however interesting as insight into Sacramento’s sausage-making process.
As it stands, the final measure is praiseworthy, as it puts the brakes on local governments’ ability to collude with special interests to more easily raise your taxes. Vote yes on Prop. 43 to make it harder to raise taxes.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Proposition 43, sponsored by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, may seem pretty basic. It is a constitutional amendment that would restore the two-thirds vote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) requirement to enact all local “special taxes” intended to fund a specific, designated purpose, such as public safety or libraries.
But the ballot measure is more accurately seen as Howard Jarvis giving voters a chance to tell the California Supreme Court to take a hike — to stop sabotaging popular state laws that create obstacles to newer and higher taxes. Just as Republican-appointed U.S. Supreme Court justices tailor their legal rulings to meet broad conservative objectives, some of the state supremes’ most important rulings feel contrived to achieve the goals of the liberal Sacramento establishment.
An obvious example is the court’s contrary rulings on citizen initiatives, which have long since lost their noble patina of being a way for voters to use “direct democracy” to overcome special interests. Instead, as political scientists and journalists have documented for decades, such measures are routinely stage-managed (https://digitalcommons.lmu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=3172&context=llr) by powerful forces — unions, business organizations and, yes, elected officials.
Sometimes the state’s justices choose to ignore this history. Sometimes they emphasize it.
In a 2017 case involving a ballot measure related to cannabis dispensaries in the city of Upland, the court, on a 5-2 vote, drastically changed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) how the judicial system interpreted voter-approved state laws, especially Proposition 13 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)) — the landmark 1978 legislation that kicked off a national taxpayer rights movement. The majority held that since the measure reached the ballot because of a citizen signature-gathering campaign — instead of the direct action of a local government body — simple majority support was necessary for enactment, not the two-thirds vote specified in Proposition 13.
Why? Because, per Justice Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar, courts must “liberally construe the public’s statewide and local initiative power.” Yet it was literally undisputed that the Upland measure reached the ballot not because of a backlash to City Hall machinations from residents but because of a well-funded effort by a cannabis trade group.
But in 2018, the state high court unanimously agreed (https://www.rstreet.org/commentary/public-sector-unions-win-big-at-the-california-supreme-court-in-getting-san-diego-pension-reforms-overturned/) that a 2012 ballot measure approved by a huge majority of San Diegans that ended defined benefit pensions for most new city hires should be invalidated (https://www.rstreet.org/commentary/public-sector-unions-win-big-at-the-california-supreme-court-in-getting-san-diego-pension-reforms-overturned/). Why? Because the fact that 116,000 city residents signed the petitions to put the measure on the ballot was tainted by the strong support of then-Mayor Jerry Sanders, who was depicted as trying to get around laws that require the city to collectively bargain changes in employment terms.
What he was trying to get around was the fact that the City Council majority, allied with unions, bitterly opposed pension changes despite compensation costs eating up a massive and growing chunk of city budgets. As former City Attorney Jan Goldsmith wrote (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2012/02/29/initiative-process-is-first-power-reserved-to-the-people/), “Never in the history of California has there ever been a requirement to negotiate with labor unions over terms of a citizens’ initiative placed on the ballot by voter signatures.”
These rulings can’t be squared. The state Supreme Court treats the citizen initiative process as a sacrosanct part of state government that must be “liberally construed” when it comes to allowing tax hikes on a simple majority vote. But when it comes to a campaign to contain pension costs, it is collective bargaining laws that must be “liberally construed” — not “the public’s statewide and local initiative power.”

By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: August 9, 2026 at 9:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: August 28, 2026 at 12:16 PM PDT

On the California Secretary of State’s website describing qualified statewide measures for the November ballot, voters will see a three-word reference to Proposition 43 referring to “Local taxes: limitation.” (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/qualified-ballot-measures) It’s ironic the initiative that has sparked the most backroom drama in years is depicted with such little fanfare.
Prop. 43 was placed on the ballot by a panicked California Legislature after a last- minute deal was struck with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to pull the association’s more sweeping Local Taxpayer Protection Act from the ballot. Despite the complicated inside-the-Capitol machinations with lobbyists and lawmakers, the resulting measure is rather simple.
If voters approve it, Prop. 43 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/aca-22.pdf) would close a court created loophole that allowed some local special taxes to evade the two-thirds vote requirement — taxes for specific items such as transit, housing, flood control and parks. Specifically, tax increases that are placed on the ballot by citizens via signature-gathering.
This change would restore the threshold to the design of 1978’s tax-limiting Proposition 13. Since then, a series of bone-headed court decisions (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/courts-widen-the-door-to-even-more-local-taxes-in-california/) determined that voters could approve citizen-driven special tax increases by a simple majority, while maintaining the two-thirds rule for special tax increases directly placed on the ballot by local governments. This loophole led to abuses, as unions served as the cat’s paw for local officials by gathering signatures to place tax increases on the ballot and pass them with less than a two-thirds vote.
So, the bottom line: Vote yes on Proposition 43, as it will impede local governments from getting around the two-thirds vote for special taxes to bail themselves out of endless budget debacles. As the economy has stumbled and local governments have burned through “free” COVID money from Washington, D.C., municipalities increasingly are turning to bonds and tax increases (https://caltax.org/2026/03/20/voters-to-decide-fate-of-80-local-tax-and-bond-measures-in-june/) .
Money is fungible. If voters approve “special” (https://flooddistrict.marincounty.gov/question/what-is-a-special-tax/) taxes, that leaves more money in the general fund to spend as usual. That typically means bigger paychecks and pensions for powerful public-employee unions. The two-thirds vote threshold is one of the few ways that California taxpayers can at least try to force their elected officials to live within their means.
That said, we’re disappointed that the final measure doesn’t include a ban and rollback of local transfer taxes. For instance, Los Angeles’ disastrous “mansion tax” (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2025-10-01/apartment-development-pipeline-dries-up-in-spite-of-demand-for-housing) not only imposes astronomical rates on Angelenos who sell pricey homes (currently a 4% tax on homes priced above $5.4 million and 5.5% on those priced above $10.9 million) — but applies to apartment and commercial properties. Predictably, that has quashed housing production in Los Angeles.
