Schaben, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images In summary The measure would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes, instead of the simple majority for citizen-led initiatives. Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure? Prop. 43 would make special taxes harder to pass. That’s the point, say anti-tax advocates

By Yue Stella Yu, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales.

In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services.

Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43, which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. 

Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups.

Californians voted in 1996 to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. 

But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify. Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority.

Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defined as any tax imposed for a specific purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reaffirmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a significant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s office interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, affirming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualified an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Office (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fiscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18

PROP 43: Two-Thirds Vote for Local Special Taxes
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2043.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Risks & Benefits
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
​​​​​​ Official ballot title: “Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”
Type: Legislative constitutional amendment (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22, Resolution Chapter 132, filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
A vote YES means: New, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters through the initiative power would need a two-thirds vote to pass, the same threshold already required when a city council or county board places a special tax on the ballot. Local governments and their voters also could not impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the limits already in the state constitution.
A vote NO means: Certain local special taxes could continue to be approved by a simple majority vote when placed on the ballot by citizen initiative.
Sponsor/proponent: Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22 as a legislative compromise. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association drove the underlying policy and its qualified citizen initiative.
On the ballot because: The legislature placed it on the ballot by a two-thirds vote of each house on June 25, 2026, as a compromise. In exchange, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its already-qualified initiative (AG No. 25-0006A1).
Full legal text: ACA 22, Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 43 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 43 would raise the vote threshold for one specific path to a new local tax. Today, when a city council or county board of supervisors asks voters to approve a special tax, meaning a tax earmarked for a specific purpose, that tax needs a two-thirds vote to pass. That requirement traces to Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996. A separate path exists. When voters themselves place a special tax on the ballot through the citizen initiative, a series of court decisions has allowed that tax to pass with a simple majority. Proposition 43 would close that gap. Beginning January 1, 2027, a voter-initiated local special tax would need the same two-thirds vote as a government-sponsored one.
The measure carries a second provision that has drawn less attention. It also bars a local government, including its electorate acting by initiative, from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property beyond the 1 percent rate that Proposition 13 already allows. This extends the existing constitutional limit so that it cannot be worked around through the initiative power.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office frames the practical effect plainly. By raising the bar for these taxes, the measure makes it harder for local governments to raise certain revenues, so local tax collections could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The office adds that the actual impact is unknown and would depend on future choices by voters and local officials.
2. The legal language
Full text: ACA 22, “Local Taxes: Limitation,” Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) (filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
Key language:
“Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.” [1, Sec. 4.5(a)]
What it amends: Adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution, the article created by Proposition 13. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own. The phrase “including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power” is the operative change, since it applies the two-thirds requirement to citizen initiatives, which recent court rulings had exempted.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22, but she did so as the vehicle for a negotiated deal rather than as a personal cause, and she has since said she opposes the measure. The policy behind it belongs to the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and its president, Jon Coupal, who had qualified a broader citizen initiative and agreed to pull it once the legislature placed this narrower version on the ballot. Opposition comes from transit, housing, and local government advocates who rely on majority-vote initiatives to fund services.
What? A two-thirds vote requirement for voter-initiated local special taxes, plus a bar on using the initiative power to impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the existing 1 percent limit.
Where? Statewide in effect, but it governs local taxes, so its bite is felt in the cities, counties, and special districts where citizen tax initiatives appear.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. The requirement applies to taxes beginning January 1, 2027.
Why? Supporters argue that a special tax is a special tax no matter who puts it on the ballot, and that letting initiatives pass earmarked taxes by a simple majority is an end run around a taxpayer protection that has stood since Proposition 13. Opponents argue that the citizen initiative is a core democratic tool and that a supermajority requirement lets a minority of voters block services the majority wants.
4. Trade-offs
For roughly two decades after Proposition 218, most people assumed every local special tax needed two-thirds approval. The California Supreme Court unsettled that assumption in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017), holding that the procedural limits Proposition 218 placed on local governments do not automatically bind voters acting through the initiative. The court itself called the change modest and left the two-thirds question open. Lower courts then took the next step, upholding several citizen special taxes that had passed with a majority rather than a two-thirds vote. That line of cases is what Proposition 43 would overturn.
The trade-off is real on both sides. The measure closes what supporters see as a loophole that lets organized campaigns pass targeted taxes with less consensus than the state constitution otherwise demands. A two-thirds rule protects the minority who bear the tax, and it forces broad agreement before money is committed to a single purpose. But the same rule is a powerful brake. Supermajority requirements let roughly one-third of voters defeat what a majority supports, and the taxes that have passed by majority under the current rule are not abstractions. They have funded things like fire protection, health services, and open-space preservation in specific counties. Under Proposition 43 several of those recent measures would have failed despite winning majority support.
There is also a worthwhile point about scope. Proposition 43 is deliberately narrower than the initiative it replaced. The original Howard Jarvis measure would also have restricted certain charter-city real estate transfer taxes and would have reached backward to invalidate some taxes already in place. ACA 22 drops both of those features and applies only going forward. Voters weighing this measure are voting on the prospective threshold change and the ad valorem limit, not on the more sweeping version that was withdrawn.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It restores a single, consistent rule. A local special tax would need two-thirds approval regardless of whether a city council or a citizen initiative places it on the ballot, ending a distinction that turned on procedure rather than substance.
It strengthens a long-standing taxpayer protection. The two-thirds requirement for earmarked local taxes has been part of California law since Proposition 13 and Proposition 218, and the measure keeps the initiative power from bypassing it.
It is prospective and narrow. Unlike the withdrawn initiative, it does not invalidate existing taxes or add new limits on real estate transfer taxes, which reduces the risk of disruptively unwinding revenue already budgeted.
It adds certainty. Litigation since Upland left the majority-versus-two-thirds question unsettled for years, and a clear constitutional rule would end that ambiguity.
Potential risks
It makes it harder to fund local services. The Legislative Analyst finds local tax revenues could be lower than they otherwise would be, though the size of the effect is unknown.
It lets a minority block a majority. A tax with 60 percent support would fail, so about one-third of voters could defeat a measure the majority favors.
It narrows a core democratic tool. The citizen initiative was designed to let voters act when their elected officials will not, and the measure raises the bar specifically for that path.
Real recent examples would have failed. Several county special taxes for fire, health, and open space passed with majorities below two-thirds and would not have survived this rule.
The ad valorem provision is easy to overlook. Most coverage focuses on the vote threshold, yet the measure also writes a real property tax limit into the constitution, and its practical reach deserves scrutiny.
6. Open questions
How many recent local special taxes actually passed with between a majority and two-thirds vote, and how much revenue statewide would have been at stake under the new rule?
Does the ad valorem provision in subdivision (b) change anything on the ground, or does it mainly codify limits that courts already enforced?
Will the narrower ACA 22 satisfy the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association over time, or does the withdrawn initiative signal a broader effort to come?
How will the measure interact with the exceptions it cross-references in Article XIII C and Article XIII D, and which taxes fall inside or outside those carve-outs?
With the author now opposed to her own measure, how will the yes and no campaigns be organized and funded?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A special tax funds one specific thing, and the state constitution has long asked for two-thirds approval before a city or county can levy one. Should the same two-thirds rule apply when voters put that tax on the ballot themselves, or should the citizen initiative be a path to a simple-majority tax that elected officials could not pass on their own?
Ask which risk worries you more: A supermajority rule that lets one-third of voters block services the majority wants, or a majority rule that lets an organized campaign commit a community to a targeted tax with less consensus than the constitution otherwise requires?

Photo by Allen J. Schaben, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images In summary The measure would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes, instead of the simple majority for citizen-led initiatives. Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure? Prop. 43 would make special taxes harder to pass. That’s the point, say anti-tax advocates

By Yue Stella Yu, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales.

In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services.

Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43, which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. 

Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups.

Californians voted in 1996 to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. 

But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify. Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority.

Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defined as any tax imposed for a specific purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reaffirmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a significant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s office interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, affirming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualified an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Office (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fiscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18

Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?

While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.
Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Even as Mayor Daniel Lurie warns of an impending doom loop for Muni if voters don’t approve the Prop H parcel tax (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-h-muni-san-francisco-22456325.php) in November, his administration offered city workers, including Muni drivers, 12% raises over the next four years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/sf-union-contracts-raise-city-workers-22422968.php), with a promise of no layoffs.
These examples point to an uncomfortable truth: Ballot measures are increasingly seen as cash grabs. Policymakers often feel they have no choice but to grant unsustainable salary increases and benefits — because they can pay for them with bottomless ballot campaigns.
Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.

Prop
43
CA
Prop
43
|
Constitutional Amendment
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services
Requires two-thirds voter approval to impose, extend, or increase special taxes, specifically eliminating the ability for a citizen initiative to qualify with a simple majority vote.
SPUR's Recommendation
SPUR has consistently called for reforming Prop. 13 and opposed onerous new restrictions on the government’s ability to raise needed revenue. Prop. 43 would take the state in the opposite direction. The measure would cement and expand Prop. 13's legacy by amending the California Constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for imposing or extending any special tax. It would undermine both the democratic principle of majority rule and one of the few remaining pathways for funding important services.
Vote NO
What Prop. 43 Would Do
Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote of the electorate to approve all special taxes, whether placed on the ballot through citizen initiative (voter signatures) or by government officials.
Proposition 13 in 1978 amended the California constitution to limit local governments’ ability to impose, extend, or increase special taxes (taxes dedicated to a specific purpose) by requiring a minimum two-thirds approval by voters. In 2017, the California Supreme Court ruled that taxes placed on the ballot by voters through signature gathering were not subject to this same two-thirds requirement. Prop. 43 seeks to overturn the 2017 decision and amend the constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval requirement for any new, extended, or increased local special tax, regardless of whether the initiative was placed on the ballot by local government officials or through a voter initiative.
The Backstory
Prop. 43 is the latest proposal in a decades-long series of amendments to the California Constitution that have significantly limited local governments' ability to fund projects and services by imposing new taxes. In 1978, Prop. 13 capped property tax rates at 1% of assessed value and established the initial two-thirds voter requirement to approve special taxes. In 2017, however, the California Supreme Court clarified in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (Upland) that many of the key provisions in the California Constitution restricting the imposition of new taxes applied only to proposals put forward by the government. Consequently, the Upland decision established that new special tax measures submitted through citizen initiative required only a 50% plus one vote majority to pass rather than two-thirds approval. 1 Since that decision, a number of local special taxes in California have passed with a simple majority after being placed on the ballot through voter initiative. Such measures account for only a small minority of revenue measures statewide.
Prop. 43 would establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for new special taxes regardless of how they were placed on the ballot. The California Legislature placed the proposition on the ballot after reaching a compromise with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, which had another, similar proposal to amend the California Constitution. 2 That proposal had qualified for the November 2026 ballot through a voter signature-gathering campaign. The compromise sidelines some of the more complex issues in the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association’s proposed amendment and instead offers a simplified amendment focused only on the voter threshold.
Prop. 43 requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Prop. 43 would make it significantly more difficult to raise revenues for local government services and projects by requiring a higher approval threshold. It is likely that the resulting fiscal impacts to government, in the form of unfunded programs or expiring taxes that can no longer be renewed, would fall most heavily on lower-income residents and people of color. In the Bay Area, for example, the citizen initiative process has recently been used to propose taxes to support transit operations and has been discussed as a potential future pathway to place a regional affordable housing bond before the voters. Transit operations and affordable housing are both examples of government expenditures that disproportionately benefit lower-income residents and people of color and that will be difficult to sustain without viable approaches to securing new revenues.
Additionally, placing broad restrictions on how the electorate can raise taxes can drive the government to seek other, less equitable sources of revenue. The severe limitations Prop. 13 placed on property taxes, for example, have, among other factors, helped drive local governments to increasingly rely on sales taxes, a much more regressive revenue source.
Pros
Prop. 43 would simplify existing law and establish a consistent, uniform voter threshold for imposing, extending, or increasing new special taxes.
The measure would maintain the 50% plus one vote threshold for passing general taxes (those not dedicated to a specific purpose).
Cons
Prop. 43 would undermine the basic principle of majority rule by imposing a heightened approval threshold on certain voter-proposed initiatives.
The measure would continue and expand on the legacy of Prop. 13, a law that has profoundly distorted California’s tax structure, fueled wealth inequality, and exacerbated the state’s housing challenges by disincentivizing home sales and turnover.
It would eliminate one of the few viable ways to raise local revenues at a time when local governments' fiscal needs are especially acute.

California’s Proposition 43 Adds a New Chapter to State’s History of Local Tax Limits
Aravind Boddupalli
Display Date
October 27, 2026
Next month, California voters will decide whether to require a two-thirds vote for voter-initiated local special taxes, or taxes dedicated to a specific purpose.
Proposition 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) would reverse a series of court decisions (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2021/a157983.html) that have allowed these measures to pass with a simple majority, raising their approval threshold to the same one that local lawmakers face to enact these taxes. If passed, it would apply to measures placed on ballots on or after January 1, 2027.
While cities, counties, and special districts provide essential services, including fire protection, roads, parks, and libraries, their ability to raise taxes is governed by a complicated set of statewide rules. Proposition 43 could further constrain local governments’ ability to raise revenue, even for services supported by a majority of voters.
California’s fiscal history and comparisons with other states offer some perspective on what the change could mean for local governments and the communities they serve.
California's fiscal rules are nearly 50 years in the making
Proposition 43 joins a lineage of statewide measures (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Detail/2669) that reshaped local public finances starting in the late 1970s. A few notable examples:
Proposition 13 (1978) capped property tax rates and required two-thirds voter approval for local special taxes, which later came to be defined as taxes dedicated to special purposes.
Proposition 218 (1996) added restrictions on local governments' ability to raise revenue, including new simple majority voter-approval requirements for new general taxes and property-related fees.
Proposition 39 (2000) lowered the voter threshold for qualifying school facility bonds from two-thirds to 55 percent, moving in the opposite direction.
Proposition 26 (2010) broadened the definition of taxes subject to voter approval.
The result is a complicated set of institutional rules where revenue changes face different voter-approval requirements depending on their type, how revenue will be used, and whether voters or legislators placed the proposal on the ballot.
California is not the only state revisiting supermajority requirements in November. Voters in South Dakota and Utah (https://www.multistate.us/elections/ballot-measure?id=21126) will consider measures that would require higher approval thresholds for certain tax or constitutional changes. But California's debate is different: It centers on voter-initiated local tax measures rather than statewide tax initiatives or statewide constitutional amendments.
The California Budget and Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/) identifies several recent voter-initiated special taxes that passed with a simple majority vote. Examples include San Francisco’s tax on commercial landlords to raise funds for child care and early education, and Fresno’s increase of its local sales tax rate to fund community parks.
What the revenue patterns reveal
According to TPC’s analysis of the 2024 Census Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances (https://state-local-finance-data.taxpolicycenter.org/pages.cfm), California ranked 37 th among states on the share of local general revenue coming from own-source revenues, like taxes, fees, or charges, rather than federal or state government transfers (Figure 1).
Since 1977, just before Proposition 13 began reshaping California's local finances, growth in local own-source revenue has trailed growth in state own-source revenue, although some of this reflects different tax bases at each government level, including the state's reliance on income taxes and local governments' heavier reliance on property taxes and fees (Figure 2).
Together, these figures suggest that California's local governments remain somewhat reliant on state decisions and intergovernmental funding streams. However, local governments continue to deliver many public services. This disconnect can weaken efficiency and accountability, as noted (https://lao.ca.gov/analysis_1993/MGMS_reprint_02-93.html) by the state's Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO).
And, if Proposition 43 makes it more challenging for local governments to raise revenues, local lawmakers may need to increase general taxes, reduce government spending, or look to state lawmakers to help foot their bills. Unlike special taxes, general taxes are not earmarked to be spent for a particular purpose. Voters who support a tax that specifically pays for child care or community parks may be less willing to support a general tax that goes into a government's general fund and could be spent across a wide range of activities.
Further, localities within California differ substantially in wealth, economic opportunity, and fiscal capacity. Jurisdictions with stronger property tax bases and local economies can often generate more revenue from the same available tax policy than communities with fewer resources (https://www.gfoa.org/materials/addressing-resource-inequities). If dedicated local revenues from special taxes are harder to secure, those disparities in fiscal capacity and maintenance of services between poorer and wealthy jurisdictions could widen, raising potential equity (https://taxpolicycenter.org/publications/state-and-local-government-revenues-and-racial-disparities) concerns (https://taxpolicycenter.org/publications/more-than-fines-and-fees-incorporating-equity-city-revenue-strategies).
California has seen before how voting rules affect tax measures
Prior research (https://www.ppic.org/publication/fiscal-effects-of-voter-approval-requirements-on-local-governments/) found that voter approval rates vary considerably by type of revenue measure, with transportation, fire protection, and education-related measures receiving the most support.
And after Proposition 39 lowered the approval threshold for school facility bond measures in 2000, passage rates increased by nearly 30 percent, according to the LAO (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Detail/2978), even though average share of voters supporting the measures remained roughly flat.
California’s voting rules create a contradiction
Voters often prefer taxes dedicated to a specific purpose (https://www.californiacityfinance.com/ReformVoteSwap.pdf), yet California generally requires higher approval thresholds for those taxes than for general taxes.
Proposition 43 would extend the two-thirds approval requirement, which currently applies to local lawmakers, to voters who propose local special taxes. Supporters could argue that requiring broader agreement protects taxpayers from increases that lack widespread support. But the higher threshold would also make it harder to pass tax measures that a majority of voters do support.
California’s history suggests that voter-approval thresholds matter. The question facing voters in November is whether requiring broader support for local special taxes is worth potentially limiting communities’ ability to raise revenue for public services.

Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?

While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)

Article continues below this ad
Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.

Article continues below this ad
When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.

Article continues below this ad
Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.
Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Even as Mayor Daniel Lurie warns of an impending doom loop for Muni if voters don’t approve the Prop H parcel tax (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-h-muni-san-francisco-22456325.php) in November, his administration offered city workers, including Muni drivers, 12% raises over the next four years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/sf-union-contracts-raise-city-workers-22422968.php), with a promise of no layoffs.
These examples point to an uncomfortable truth: Ballot measures are increasingly seen as cash grabs. Policymakers often feel they have no choice but to grant unsustainable salary increases and benefits — because they can pay for them with bottomless ballot campaigns.
Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.

Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?
