Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.
Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Even as Mayor Daniel Lurie warns of an impending doom loop for Muni if voters don’t approve the Prop H parcel tax (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-h-muni-san-francisco-22456325.php) in November, his administration offered city workers, including Muni drivers, 12% raises over the next four years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/sf-union-contracts-raise-city-workers-22422968.php), with a promise of no layoffs.
These examples point to an uncomfortable truth: Ballot measures are increasingly seen as cash grabs. Policymakers often feel they have no choice but to grant unsustainable salary increases and benefits — because they can pay for them with bottomless ballot campaigns.
Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.
About Opinion
The editorial positions of The Chronicle, including election recommendations, represent the consensus of the editorial board , consisting of the publisher, the editorial page editor and staff members of the opinion pages. Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
We don’t support Prop 43 because it further cements a broken system. But ultimately, we won’t oppose it, either. If the measure passes, perhaps it will finally force California to build the coherent system of taxation we so clearly need.

Prop

CA
Prop
43
|
Constitutional Amendment
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services
Requires two-thirds voter approval to impose, extend, or increase special taxes, specifically eliminating the ability for a citizen initiative to qualify with a simple majority vote.
SPUR's Recommendation
SPUR has consistently called for reforming Prop. 13 and opposed onerous new restrictions on the government’s ability to raise needed revenue. Prop. 43 would take the state in the opposite direction. The measure would cement and expand Prop. 13's legacy by amending the California Constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for imposing or extending any special tax. It would undermine both the democratic principle of majority rule and one of the few remaining pathways for funding important services.
Vote NO
What Prop. 43 Would Do
Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote of the electorate to approve all special taxes, whether placed on the ballot through citizen initiative (voter signatures) or by government officials.
Proposition 13 in 1978 amended the California constitution to limit local governments’ ability to impose, extend, or increase special taxes (taxes dedicated to a specific purpose) by requiring a minimum two-thirds approval by voters. In 2017, the California Supreme Court ruled that taxes placed on the ballot by voters through signature gathering were not subject to this same two-thirds requirement. Prop. 43 seeks to overturn the 2017 decision and amend the constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval requirement for any new, extended, or increased local special tax, regardless of whether the initiative was placed on the ballot by local government officials or through a voter initiative.
The Backstory
Prop. 43 is the latest proposal in a decades-long series of amendments to the California Constitution that have significantly limited local governments' ability to fund projects and services by imposing new taxes. In 1978, Prop. 13 capped property tax rates at 1% of assessed value and established the initial two-thirds voter requirement to approve special taxes. In 2017, however, the California Supreme Court clarified in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (Upland) that many of the key provisions in the California Constitution restricting the imposition of new taxes applied only to proposals put forward by the government. Consequently, the Upland decision established that new special tax measures submitted through citizen initiative required only a 50% plus one vote majority to pass rather than two-thirds approval. 1 Since that decision, a number of local special taxes in California have passed with a simple majority after being placed on the ballot through voter initiative. Such measures account for only a small minority of revenue measures statewide.
Prop. 43 would establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for new special taxes regardless of how they were placed on the ballot. The California Legislature placed the proposition on the ballot after reaching a compromise with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, which had another, similar proposal to amend the California Constitution. 2 That proposal had qualified for the November 2026 ballot through a voter signature-gathering campaign. The compromise sidelines some of the more complex issues in the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association’s proposed amendment and instead offers a simplified amendment focused only on the voter threshold.
Prop. 43 requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Prop. 43 would make it significantly more difficult to raise revenues for local government services and projects by requiring a higher approval threshold. It is likely that the resulting fiscal impacts to government, in the form of unfunded programs or expiring taxes that can no longer be renewed, would fall most heavily on lower-income residents and people of color. In the Bay Area, for example, the citizen initiative process has recently been used to propose taxes to support transit operations and has been discussed as a potential future pathway to place a regional affordable housing bond before the voters. Transit operations and affordable housing are both examples of government expenditures that disproportionately benefit lower-income residents and people of color and that will be difficult to sustain without viable approaches to securing new revenues.
Additionally, placing broad restrictions on how the electorate can raise taxes can drive the government to seek other, less equitable sources of revenue. The severe limitations Prop. 13 placed on property taxes, for example, have, among other factors, helped drive local governments to increasingly rely on sales taxes, a much more regressive revenue source.
Pros
Prop. 43 would simplify existing law and establish a consistent, uniform voter threshold for imposing, extending, or increasing new special taxes.
The measure would maintain the 50% plus one vote threshold for passing general taxes (those not dedicated to a specific purpose).
Cons
Prop. 43 would undermine the basic principle of majority rule by imposing a heightened approval threshold on certain voter-proposed initiatives.
The measure would continue and expand on the legacy of Prop. 13, a law that has profoundly distorted California’s tax structure, fueled wealth inequality, and exacerbated the state’s housing challenges by disincentivizing home sales and turnover.
It would eliminate one of the few viable ways to raise local revenues at a time when local governments' fiscal needs are especially acute.

California’s Proposition 43 Adds a New Chapter to State’s History of Local Tax Limits
Aravind Boddupalli
Display Date
October 27, 2026
Next month, California voters will decide whether to require a two-thirds vote for voter-initiated local special taxes, or taxes dedicated to a specific purpose.
Proposition 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) would reverse a series of court decisions (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2021/a157983.html) that have allowed these measures to pass with a simple majority, raising their approval threshold to the same one that local lawmakers face to enact these taxes. If passed, it would apply to measures placed on ballots on or after January 1, 2027.
While cities, counties, and special districts provide essential services, including fire protection, roads, parks, and libraries, their ability to raise taxes is governed by a complicated set of statewide rules. Proposition 43 could further constrain local governments’ ability to raise revenue, even for services supported by a majority of voters.
California’s fiscal history and comparisons with other states offer some perspective on what the change could mean for local governments and the communities they serve.
California's fiscal rules are nearly 50 years in the making
Proposition 43 joins a lineage of statewide measures (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Detail/2669) that reshaped local public finances starting in the late 1970s. A few notable examples:
Proposition 13 (1978) capped property tax rates and required two-thirds voter approval for local special taxes, which later came to be defined as taxes dedicated to special purposes.
Proposition 218 (1996) added restrictions on local governments' ability to raise revenue, including new simple majority voter-approval requirements for new general taxes and property-related fees.
Proposition 39 (2000) lowered the voter threshold for qualifying school facility bonds from two-thirds to 55 percent, moving in the opposite direction.
Proposition 26 (2010) broadened the definition of taxes subject to voter approval.
The result is a complicated set of institutional rules where revenue changes face different voter-approval requirements depending on their type, how revenue will be used, and whether voters or legislators placed the proposal on the ballot.
California is not the only state revisiting supermajority requirements in November. Voters in South Dakota and Utah (https://www.multistate.us/elections/ballot-measure?id=21126) will consider measures that would require higher approval thresholds for certain tax or constitutional changes. But California's debate is different: It centers on voter-initiated local tax measures rather than statewide tax initiatives or statewide constitutional amendments.
The California Budget and Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/) identifies several recent voter-initiated special taxes that passed with a simple majority vote. Examples include San Francisco’s tax on commercial landlords to raise funds for child care and early education, and Fresno’s increase of its local sales tax rate to fund community parks.
What the revenue patterns reveal
According to TPC’s analysis of the 2024 Census Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances (https://state-local-finance-data.taxpolicycenter.org/pages.cfm), California ranked 37 th among states on the share of local general revenue coming from own-source revenues, like taxes, fees, or charges, rather than federal or state government transfers (Figure 1).
Since 1977, just before Proposition 13 began reshaping California's local finances, growth in local own-source revenue has trailed growth in state own-source revenue, although some of this reflects different tax bases at each government level, including the state's reliance on income taxes and local governments' heavier reliance on property taxes and fees (Figure 2).
Together, these figures suggest that California's local governments remain somewhat reliant on state decisions and intergovernmental funding streams. However, local governments continue to deliver many public services. This disconnect can weaken efficiency and accountability, as noted (https://lao.ca.gov/analysis_1993/MGMS_reprint_02-93.html) by the state's Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO).
And, if Proposition 43 makes it more challenging for local governments to raise revenues, local lawmakers may need to increase general taxes, reduce government spending, or look to state lawmakers to help foot their bills. Unlike special taxes, general taxes are not earmarked to be spent for a particular purpose. Voters who support a tax that specifically pays for child care or community parks may be less willing to support a general tax that goes into a government's general fund and could be spent across a wide range of activities.
Further, localities within California differ substantially in wealth, economic opportunity, and fiscal capacity. Jurisdictions with stronger property tax bases and local economies can often generate more revenue from the same available tax policy than communities with fewer resources (https://www.gfoa.org/materials/addressing-resource-inequities). If dedicated local revenues from special taxes are harder to secure, those disparities in fiscal capacity and maintenance of services between poorer and wealthy jurisdictions could widen, raising potential equity (https://taxpolicycenter.org/publications/state-and-local-government-revenues-and-racial-disparities) concerns (https://taxpolicycenter.org/publications/more-than-fines-and-fees-incorporating-equity-city-revenue-strategies).
California has seen before how voting rules affect tax measures
Prior research (https://www.ppic.org/publication/fiscal-effects-of-voter-approval-requirements-on-local-governments/) found that voter approval rates vary considerably by type of revenue measure, with transportation, fire protection, and education-related measures receiving the most support.
And after Proposition 39 lowered the approval threshold for school facility bond measures in 2000, passage rates increased by nearly 30 percent, according to the LAO (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Detail/2978), even though average share of voters supporting the measures remained roughly flat.
California’s voting rules create a contradiction
Voters often prefer taxes dedicated to a specific purpose (https://www.californiacityfinance.com/ReformVoteSwap.pdf), yet California generally requires higher approval thresholds for those taxes than for general taxes.
Proposition 43 would extend the two-thirds approval requirement, which currently applies to local lawmakers, to voters who propose local special taxes. Supporters could argue that requiring broader agreement protects taxpayers from increases that lack widespread support. But the higher threshold would also make it harder to pass tax measures that a majority of voters do support.
California’s history suggests that voter-approval thresholds matter. The question facing voters in November is whether requiring broader support for local special taxes is worth potentially limiting communities’ ability to raise revenue for public services.

Home (https://calbudgetcenter.org/) / Resources (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/) / Should California Voters Approve Proposition 43?
Issue Brief
Should California Voters Approve Proposition 43?
What the Supermajority Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives Would Mean for California Communities
August 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would require that at least two-thirds of local voters approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax, starting on January 1, 2027. As communities across California are facing substantial challenges and uncertainties, this measure would make it harder for local voters to raise revenues to support local public services and give outsized power to a small share of voters. Approval of the measure would decrease the likelihood that local governments meet the needs of their residents and could increase hardship in some communities throughout the state.
table of contents
What Would Proposition 43 Do?
Glossary of Key Terms
What Are the Current Vote Requirements for Local Revenue Increases in California?
What Services Do Local Governments in California Provide?
How Do Local Governments Raise Revenue?
How Would Proposition 43 Affect California Communities?
Proposition 43 Supporters and Opponents
What Would Proposition 43 Do?
This measure would require at least two-thirds of local voters to approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax. The measure would apply to initiatives placed on a local ballot on or after January 1, 2027.
This new supermajority vote requirement would apply to special tax voter initiatives raising revenue for many types of local governments, including cities, counties, special districts, and other local or regional government entity. 1 (javascript:void(0)) Under California’s Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C), all taxes levied by special districts are considered “special taxes,” so Prop. 43’s two-thirds vote requirement would apply to any taxes placed on the ballot by voters to generate revenues for special districts as well as city and county taxes for dedicated purposes.
Glossary of Key Terms
General tax
Local voter initiative process
Parcel tax
Simple majority vote
Special tax
Supermajority vote
General tax
A tax that is levied by a city or county and that may be spent on any program or service. All non-property taxes that cities and counties may levy can be imposed as general taxes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) . A general tax may be approved by a simple majority of local voters, regardless of whether it is placed on the ballot by the local government entity or by a local voter initiative.
Local voter initiative process
Gives residents of a city or a county the power to propose changes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2011.&article=II) to local ordinances. This process involves a number of steps, including drafting a ballot measure, circulating petitions, and gathering the required signatures.
Parcel tax
A tax on a parcel of property that is not based on the property value. This tax is generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square-foot or per-room basis. Parcel taxes can be levied by cities, counties, school districts, community college districts, and most special districts. Parcel taxes are always considered to be special taxes for the purpose of determining voter-approval requirements.
Simple majority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive support from at least half of voters plus one additional voter (50%+1) in order to be approved.
Special tax
Includes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) 1) parcel taxes, 2) city or county taxes (excluding property taxes) dedicated to specific purposes, and 3) taxes (excluding property taxes) levied by special purpose districts — that is, special districts, K-12 school districts, and community college districts.
Supermajority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive more than a simple majority vote, such as three-fifths or two-thirds, in order to be approved.
What Are the Current Vote Requirements for Local Revenue Increases in California?
California’s Constitution has a complex set of rules governing how local governments can raise taxes and other types of revenue. These rules were put in place by statewide ballot measures over the past several decades (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Major%20Milestones%20in%20the%20Development%20of%20Voter%E2%80%93Approval%20Requirements%20for%20Local%20Taxes), beginning with Prop. 13 in 1978 and followed by other measures creating additional restrictions on local revenue-raising capacity, including Prop. 62 (1986) and Prop. 218 (1996).
These rules apply to local measures to create new taxes as well as to increase or extend any existing tax.
Tax measures proposed by local governments — such as city councils or county boards of supervisors — must go on the ballot and be approved by voters. Current voter-approval thresholds differ depending on the type of tax that would be raised:
A general tax requires only a simple majority vote to pass, with the revenue available for any program or service.
A special tax requires a two-thirds vote to pass, and includes a tax dedicated to a specific purpose.
Special taxes proposed through the local voter initiative process are subject to different rules. In recent years, a series of court decisions (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2021/a157983.html) have clarified that the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes in the state Constitution does not apply to special tax measures placed on the ballot by local voter initiative. Therefore, both general taxes and special taxes proposed by voters can be approved with a simple majority vote . 2 (javascript:void(0)) Several cases involving special tax voter initiatives that were approved with a simple majority vote were appealed to the California Supreme Court, but the Supreme Court denied review of the appellate court decisions, allowing these decisions to stand. A variety of special tax initiatives have been approved over the past several years with a simple majority vote, such as:
San Francisco’s Measure C in November 2018, creating a tax on commercial landlords to raise funds for child care and early education, which passed with 51% of the vote.
Fresno’s Measure P in November 2018, increasing the local sales tax rate to fund community parks, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Los Angeles’ Measure ULA in November 2022, creating a property transfer tax on sales of high-value property to raise funds for affordable housing development and homelessness service, which passed with 58% of the vote.
Madera County’s Measure T in November 2024, renewing a local sales tax rate to fund transportation projects, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Certain types of local taxes are always classified as special taxes for the purposes of voter approval requirements. This includes:
Taxes levied by special-purpose districts, including school districts, community college districts, and special districts.
Parcel taxes, which are taxes on parcels of property that are not based on the property value . These taxes are generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square foot or per-room basis.
What Services Do Local Governments in California Provide?
Californians in every community across the state benefit from services provided by local governments. Local services help keep people safe and healthy by providing fire protection, law enforcement, public health services, hospitals and emergency services, road safety, and more. Local governments also provide educational and recreational spaces like public libraries, public parks, and playgrounds.
Californians experiencing economic insecurity, food security, or who don’t have access to private health insurance can access financial assistance, food assistance, and health care because counties are there to administer public health and economic security programs. Cities can support the development of affordable housing to ensure more of their residents can afford a safe place to live.
The services provided by California’s local governments vary according to the type of entity (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/who_does_what.pdf):
Counties administer health and human services programs such as Medi-Cal (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/medi-cal/) health coverage, CalFresh (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calfresh/) food assistance, and CalWORKs (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calworks/) cash assistance for families. Counties also provide public health, behavioral health, and child welfare services. Additionally, counties are responsible (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/california-county-budget-process-guide/) for overseeing the local justice system and courts, administering elections, and providing municipal services like sewer systems and trash pick-up in unincorporated areas.
Cities provide a variety of municipal services such as fire protection, housing and urban planning, parks and recreation, libraries, street repair, water and sewer systems, and law enforcement — although some of these services may be provided by special districts in some areas.
Special districts provide specialized services such as fire protection, water, electricity, parks and recreation, transit, hospitals, and other health care services.
Regional entities such as Joint Powers Authorities and Councils of Government coordinate policy and service provision across regions spanning multiple cities or counties, such as regional transportation authorities.
How Do Local Governments Raise Revenue?
Local governments in California rely on a variety of revenue sources, including transfers from the state and federal governments, allocations of local property taxes, and various other taxes, service charges, assessments, and fees.
Most types of local governments receive some revenues from the local property tax, capped at 1% by Prop. 13 (1978). Property taxes are collected by counties and the revenues are allocated (https://propertytax.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2026/revenue/0/entity_type?vis=pieChart) to support city and county governments, school districts, community college districts, and special districts in accordance with formulas established in state law. Local governments and voters cannot increase property taxes beyond the 1% rate, except to finance infrastructure bonds. 3 (javascript:void(0)) Property tax increases to support school infrastructure bonds can generally be approved by 55% of local voters. All other property taxes for infrastructure bonds must be approved by two-thirds of voters.

Other common types of taxes supporting local services include sales taxes (known as transactions and use taxes at the local level), taxes on hotel stays (known as transient occupancy taxes), property transfer taxes, utility user taxes, and business license taxes.
The revenues that make up local government budgets vary by the type of entity (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Local%20Governments%20Levy%20Many%20Types%20of%20Taxes), and the legal authority to raise taxes (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/resources__Revenues_and_Responsibilities.pdf) also differs by government type. Cities and counties have fairly broad authority to raise a variety of taxes — with voter approval — while special districts have more limited authority. These districts are largely limited to parcel taxes — a tax on parcels of land not based on their value — as a source of discretionary revenue, although some can levy district sales taxes and certain other types of taxes.
More than half of county-level revenues (https://counties.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/category?vis=pieChart) statewide come from the state and federal governments and local property taxes. Other types of taxes make up a small share of total county revenues — generally less than 3%. Common types of taxes levied by counties include sales taxes, property transfer taxes, taxes on hotel stays, and utility user taxes.
City-level revenues (https://cities.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/subcategory_1?vis=pieChart) primarily come from service charges for municipal functions — such as electricity, water, and sewer services — and various taxes. These two categories generally each make up around one-third of total city revenues statewide. Local property tax revenues and sales taxes are the largest sources of tax revenues for cities, each representing about one-quarter of tax revenues. Other major tax revenue sources for cities include taxes on hotel stays, utility user taxes, and business license taxes.
Special district revenues (https://districts.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/subcategory_2?vis=pieChart) come largely from customer service charges for the service provided by the district, local property taxes, and certain other taxes and assessments, depending on the type of district. 4 (javascript:void(0)) The composition of special district revenues depends on the type of special district (https://sgf.senate.ca.gov/sites/sgf.senate.ca.gov/files/special_district_facts_2016.pdf). Enterprise districts provide services to customers for a charge and operate similar to businesses, being largely financed by user charges. Examples of enterprise districts include health care districts, airport districts, water districts, and other utility districts. Non-enterprise districts provide benefits to entire communities — such as fire protection and road repair services — and are primarily funded by property taxes and other types of taxes and assessments. As noted above, taxes levied by special districts are always considered special taxes so they require approval of two-thirds of voters in the district, unless they are placed on the ballot by voters.
How Would Proposition 43 Affect California Communities?
Proposition 43 Would Make It More Difficult for Communities to Generate Revenues to Meet Local Needs
California already imposes high barriers to raising local revenues by requiring all special taxes levied by local governments to be approved by two-thirds of voters instead of a simple majority, and by classifying certain types of taxes — parcel taxes and taxes levied by special districts and school districts — as special taxes subject to higher vote requirements. Extending the two-thirds vote requirement to voter-initiated special tax proposals, as Prop. 43 proposes, would decrease the likelihood that these measures would pass, even if a significant majority of local voters support the measure and the services that the new revenues would fund.
In contrast to the high bar for raising taxes, local governments do not need voter approval to reduce services — and cuts to services often result when localities face revenue shortfalls. Yet, communities also have the option of raising revenues to help close budget gaps. If Prop. 43 passes, counties and cities would still have the ability to raise general taxes with approval from a simple majority of voters to shore up local services. However, local voters’ ability to propose new special taxes to protect or strengthen key services would be limited as local voter initiatives would become much more challenging to pass. Additionally, voters in special districts would face a higher bar to increase revenues to preserve and expand services, regardless of whether the funds would be targeted to specific programs.
Proposition 43’s Constraints on Local Revenues Would Make Things Harder for Communities Already Struggling

Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local special tax that residents place on the ballot by petition, the same threshold that already applies when a city council, county board or special district proposes one. A special tax is one whose money is dedicated to a specific purpose, such as fire protection, parks, housing or schools. Since a series of court rulings that began in 2017, voter-proposed special taxes have needed only a simple majority. Prop 43 would end that for measures approved from January 1, 2027, and it leaves every tax already on the books in place.

Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote for voter-proposed local special taxes:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a single section, 4.5, to Article XIII A of the California Constitution, the article voters created with Proposition 13 in 1978. Its first subdivision reads: "Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax" unless it is "submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote."
Three parts of that sentence do the work:
"Including the electorate … exercising the initiative power." These words bring residents who propose a tax by petition under the same rule as the officials who govern them. Article II is the article that grants the initiative power, and the "notwithstanding" clause sets it aside for this purpose.
"Impose, extend, or increase." The rule covers new taxes, higher rates and renewals. A voter-proposed special tax that passed by majority before 2027 keeps running, but extending it past its end date or raising its rate would need two-thirds.
"Special tax." The measure borrows its definitions from Article XIII C, the article added by Proposition 218 in 1996: a special tax is one "imposed for specific purposes," and a "local government" is any county, city, city and county, including a charter city or county, any special district, or any other local or regional governmental entity. General taxes, whose money can be spent on anything, still pass by majority no matter who proposes them.
A second subdivision states that no local government, "including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose ad valorem taxes on real property," except the property tax Article XIII D already allows. The Legislative Analyst's Office does not discuss this clause as a separate change, and neither ballot argument mentions it.
The Attorney General's summary puts the timing plainly: the measure "applies to voter-proposed ballot measures approved after January 1, 2027." Local tax measures on the November 3 ballot are still decided under the current rules.

Supermajority requirements are undemocratic. So is Proposition 43
Proposition 43 on the Nov. 3 ballot would require that special taxes proposed through the citizen-initiative process earn two-thirds of votes in order to pass.
California’s next governor will be decided by a simple majority of voters in the Nov. election. As will the next mayor of Los Angeles, and whether the state will require voters to show ID at the polls in the future.
That’s the way most elections work: Decisions big and small come down to the preference of most voters. This is the majority-rule principle in action, and it ensures that every vote carries equal weight.
In California, there’s one glaring exception. Under the state constitution, local special tax measures that fund a specific purpose must earn two-thirds of the votes to pass.
This high bar makes it exceptionally difficult for cities, counties, school districts and other local governments to raise taxes to pay for things like transit projects and homeless services.
In recent years, however, several courts have ruled that taxes proposed by citizen initiative need only a simple majority to pass, as opposed to ones placed on the ballot by governing bodies.
This cleared the way for new taxes to pass with less than 66.7%, including Measure ULA, the city of Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” in 2022. That would change under Proposition 43, a constitutional amendment placed on the Nov. 3 statewide ballot by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association as part of a deal with state lawmakers in which both sides backed away from more extreme tax proposals. If a majority of voters (irony alert!) approves Proposition 43, the supermajority rule would apply to future initiative special tax measures.
Supporters believe that was the intent of two previous anti-tax measures, Propositions 13 and 218, even if they didn’t actually spell it out.
There’s certainly some benefit to having consistency when it comes to special taxes. And proponents are right when they claim that many so-called citizen initiatives are really just sneaky workarounds by groups aligned with a local government.
Case in point, says Susan Shelley, vice president of communications of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, was Measure A, a homeless services sales tax on Los Angeles County’s 2024 ballot.
The initiative’s official proponents were organizations working on homeless services, but they appeared to be in concert with local officials (L.A. Mayor Karen Bass even boasted about writing part of it at a public event last year.) Shelley also cites Measure RTM, a proposed sales tax hike for transit projects in the Bay Area.
The Legislature created the taxing district last year with the intent of putting a sales tax on the ballot. “How is that a real citizens initiative? It’s coming from the government and it’s just using this loophole,” Shelley said.
Opponents of Proposition 43 — which include about a million civic, community, civil rights, pro-housing and transit groups, as well as labor unions and the state Democratic Party — make an important distinction between citizen and government tax measures.
They point out that citizen initiatives already have a higher obstacle to passage than those placed on the ballot by a local government because they need to gather a significant number of valid signatures, typically based on a percentage of votes cast in a recent election. At the moment, qualifying a ballot measure in L.A. city takes 139,000 valid signatures.
“If you try to stack the deck and say that you need two-thirds [of votes], that’s not a fight,” said Bill Barnes, director of campaigns and community engagement for the Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California, who signed the rebuttal in the state’s official voter guide.
He’s right. It’s unfair for a small fraction of the voters in a community to have veto power over the majority in making funding decisions for a community. It’s undemocratic as well.
That’s why I can’t vote for Proposition 43.
In fact, if there were a ballot measure to ban supermajority vote requirements, I would enthusiastically vote for it.

ca.gov/files/hearings/Jt_Informational_Hearing_ALGC.pdf) on the case quotes it. The court added a test for future cases: "Without a direct reference in the text of a provision—or a similarly clear, unambiguous indication that it was within the ambit of a provision's purpose to constrain the people's initiative power—we will not construe a provision as imposing such a limitation."
Appellate courts then applied that reasoning to special taxes. In June 2020 the First District Court of Appeal upheld San Francisco's November 2018 Proposition C, a business tax for homelessness services, reading the two-thirds requirements "as coexisting with, not displacing, the people's power to enact initiatives by majority vote." The Fifth District reached the same result for Fresno's parks tax in December 2020. The First District did so again in 2021 for two more San Francisco measures, a June 2018 commercial rent tax for child care and a parcel tax for teacher pay (https://cases.justia.com/california/court-of-appeal/2021-a160659.pdf), noting that every appellate court to address the question had agreed. The California Supreme Court declined to review the ruling on the child care tax, which had passed with about 51%, according to the San Francisco City Attorney (https://sfcityattorney.org/?p=8889).
Prop 43 answers that test in its own words. Its text names "the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power," the kind of "direct reference" the Upland court said a limit on voters would require.
Local special taxes today vs Proposition 43 and the withdrawn initiative:
Rule Today If Proposition 43 passes Withdrawn initiative #1983 (for comparison)
Special tax placed on the ballot by a city council, board or district Two-thirds vote Two-thirds vote (no change) Two-thirds vote
Special tax placed on the ballot by citizen petition Majority vote, under 2020 and 2021 appellate rulings Two-thirds vote, for measures from January 1, 2027 Two-thirds vote
General tax (money for any purpose) Majority vote Majority vote (no change) Majority vote
Special taxes already passed by majority (Measure ULA, Fresno Measure P and others) Stay in effect Stay in effect; any later extension or increase needs two-thirds Existing property-related special taxes passed below two-thirds voided two years after enactment
Charter-city real estate transfer taxes Allowed at rates each city sets Not addressed Banned beyond the statewide documentary transfer tax, including existing ones
Legislative Analyst's fiscal estimate Not applicable Local tax revenue "could be lower in the future"; amount "unknown" Annual loss of "up to a couple of billion dollars," mostly in charter cities
Four voter-initiated special taxes passed with 52% to 61%, all short of two-thirds:
The taxes that passed under the majority rule include some of the largest local revenue measures of the past decade. Four with public records of both their vote share and their citizen-initiative status:
San Francisco Proposition C (November 2018) , a gross receipts tax on large businesses for homelessness services, passed with 61.34% of 351,326 votes, according to the Court of Appeal's opinion (https://cases.justia.com/california/court-of-appeal/2020-a158645.pdf).
San Francisco Proposition G (June 2018) , a parcel tax for San Francisco Unified School District teacher pay, passed with 60.76% of 238,133 votes.
Fresno Measure P (November 2018) , a 30-year sales tax for parks estimated at $37.5 million a year, passed with 52.17%. The city first declared it failed for lack of two-thirds and then certified it as passed in February 2021 after the appellate ruling, according to the Fresno City Council's legislative file (https://agendas.fresno.gov/en/legislation/id-21-344-12830).
Los Angeles Measure ULA (November 2022) , known as the "mansion tax," adds a 4% tax on sales of real property over $5 million and 5.5% on sales of $10 million or more, "until ended by voters." It passed with 512,808 votes to 374,934, or 57.77%, according to the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder (https://results.lavote.gov/). Under a two-thirds rule it would have needed 591,828 yes votes, 79,020 more than it received. The Los Angeles Housing Department (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula) says collections began April 1, 2023, with 70% of the money going to affordable housing and 30% to homelessness prevention. CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-prop-43-election-2026/) that the thresholds, indexed to inflation, now stand at $5.3 million and $10.6 million and that the city says the tax has raised $1.4 billion.
Proposition 43's two-thirds threshold is sitting above four voter-initiated special taxes in San Francisco, Fresno and Los Angeles that passed with 52% to 61% of the vote between 2018 and 2022. Other measures followed the same path. CalMatters reports that 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax for wildfire response and emergency services in 2024, short of two-thirds. Neither campaign nor the LAO publishes a statewide count of voter-initiated special taxes passed by majority since 2017, so these examples are not a complete list.
None of these taxes would be repealed. Prop 43 applies from 2027 forward. What would change is the next one: a new citizen-proposed parcel tax, sales tax or transfer tax, or a renewal or increase of an existing one, would need two-thirds.
Proposition 43 came from a June 25 deal that replaced a broader Howard Jarvis initiative:
Prop 43 is the narrow survivor of a much larger fight. In 2024 the California Supreme Court unanimously removed the Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act, which would have raised the thresholds for approving local taxes among other changes, from that year's ballot, ruling it an invalid revision of the Constitution rather than an amendment, the law firm Hanson Bridgett reported (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publication/240620-4000-ca-supreme-court-bars-fall-ballot-measure). The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association then qualified a new initiative for 2026, the "Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13" (initiative #1983, A.G. file 25-0006). Its petition drive was paid for by Protect Prop. 13, a project of the association, according to the Secretary of State's top-funders filing (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/top-funders/1983-top-funders-01-05-26.pdf).
That initiative went much further than Prop 43. It would have required two-thirds for voter-proposed special taxes, barred charter cities from imposing real estate transfer taxes beyond the statewide documentary transfer tax, and overturned existing property-related taxes that did not meet those rules two years after passage. The LAO's 2025 analysis (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) estimated an "annual loss of revenues to local governments totaling up to a couple of billion dollars, predominantly affecting certain charter cities." That included about $300 million a year in existing parcel taxes approved with less than two-thirds, and the special-purpose transfer taxes that voters "recently" approved in Los Angeles and Santa Monica. Measure ULA was one of them.
The Legislature had its own measure on the 2026 ballot aimed at that initiative. ACA 13, passed in 2023, would have required any initiative that raises a vote threshold to pass by that same higher threshold, which in practice meant two-thirds for the Howard Jarvis measure.
Both came off the ballot on June 25, the last day an initiative could be withdrawn. The deal was announced by the initiative's proponents, Governor Gavin Newsom and legislative leaders, according to the California Special Districts Association (https://www.csda.net/blogs/morgan-leskody/2026/06/29/legislature-cuts-deal-with-vote-threshold-proponen). That day:
ACA 21 (Resolution Chapter 131) removed ACA 13 from the November ballot, according to the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/qualified-ballot-measures).
ACA 22 (Resolution Chapter 132), by Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, an Oakland Democrat, was introduced and adopted by both houses without committee hearings, according to the legislative record mirrored on LegiScan (https://legiscan.com/CA/bill/ACA22/2025). It passed the Assembly 68–2 and the Senate 35–1 and became Prop 43.
Jon Coupal , the association's president, withdrew initiative #1983 under Elections Code section 9604, according to a Secretary of State memo to county elections officials (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26167jh.pdf).
"Today the Legislature voted to make it harder to raise taxes," Coupal said (https://www.hjta.org/press-releases/taxpayers-win-in-sacramento-with-unprecedented-support-for-two-thirds-vote-requirement-to-raise-special-taxes/) in a joint release with the California Taxpayers Association. Wicks wrote the compromise language and days later said she was "adamantly opposed" to it, CalMatters reported. Her explanation, in a social media post the outlet quoted: "The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy."
LAO fiscal estimate says local tax revenue could be lower, by an unknown amount:
The LAO's analysis of Prop 43 is short. Because the measure "makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes," it says, "local governments' tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters." The ballot summary of the fiscal effect reads: "Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes."
The estimate has no dollar figure because Prop 43 touches no existing tax. Its effect depends on how many voter-proposed special taxes would win between 50% and 66.7% of the vote in future elections.
Proposition 43's Yes campaign reports $14.0 million from its top donors and the No side $6.7 million:
The Fair Political Practices Commission's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), updated October 14, shows $14.0 million from the ten largest donors to the Yes committee, "Yes on Prop 43 – The Local Taxpayer Protection Act." The California Business Roundtable Issues PAC gave $9.87 million; the FPPC lists Peter Thiel and Kim DeGeorge as its top donors. Protect Prop. 13, the Howard Jarvis project, gave $1.04 million, and the real estate companies Kilroy Realty and Douglas Emmett Properties gave $1 million each.
The No committee, "No on Prop 43: Stop the Local Taxpayer Deception Act," reports $5.6 million from its ten largest donors. The SEIU California State Council gave $1.5 million. The California Teachers Association, two carpenters' councils, two SEIU locals, the Southern California Partnership for Jobs and the California Alliance for Jobs gave $500,000 each. The California Professional Firefighters gave $365,257, and the League of California Cities' CITIPAC gave $250,000. A third committee formed for several measures, Communities for an Affordable California (Yes on 3, No on 39 and 43), adds $1.09 million, which brings the FPPC's opposition total to $6.7 million. The FPPC marks that last figure with an asterisk because, for a committee covering more than one measure, "it is not possible to determine the amount of the contribution that was spent specifically on the campaign for any particular measure."
The Secretary of State's contribution tally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-43-aca-22-wicks-local-taxes-limitation-res-ch-132-2026), which counts all reported contributions through October 6 rather than the largest donors, shows $10.0 million for the two Yes committees and $8.0 million for the two committees opposing it. The Million Voters Project's committee also opposes Proposition 39 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/yes-voter-id-laws-are-on-the-california-ballot-proposition-39s-rules-costs-and-court-fights/) and supports Proposition 3 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-millionaire-tax-proposition-3/).
The arguments over Proposition 43 pit "closing loopholes" against "minority rule":
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by the presidents of the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, says "court decisions created loopholes that allow special interests to impose massive new tax increases by circumventing the taxpayer protections voters approved." It says local governments "have imposed over 2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade" and that "some cities now charge real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%," which on a $900,000 home "would cost a homeowner $54,000 simply for selling their house." The argument does not say how many of those 2,000 taxes were voter-proposed special taxes, the only kind Prop 43 affects. The rebuttal, signed by Coupal and others, calls the Legislature's vote "nearly unanimous" and says it shows "activist courts exceeded voters' intent."
The No argument, signed by the presidents of the California Professional Firefighters and the California School Employees Association and the executive director of SEIU's Nurse Alliance, says Prop 43 "makes it harder for you to fund critical services like police and fire departments, fix and repair local roads, staff our local schools or backfill federal healthcare cuts." Its central objection is arithmetic: the measure lets "just over one-third of voters" block "what nearly 67% want," and "makes their NO vote count twice as much as a YES vote." It says "corporate donors who spend big in elections will benefit most." The No rebuttal adds that Prop 43 "doesn't cut your taxes a penny."
The campaigns' claims go beyond the guide. The No campaign's release of Governor Newsom's statement says communities "would have lost nearly $3 billion a year" if Prop 43 had been law, a figure the LAO does not estimate. The guide notes that ballot arguments "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
Proposition 43 trails in both public polls, and Governor Newsom opposes it:
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters, fielded September 4–10, found 43% yes, 51% no and 6% undecided. Republicans support it 61% to 35%. Democrats oppose it 60% to 33%, and independents 51% to 43%. Homeowners split 48% yes to 47% no, while renters oppose it 61% to 33%. Only 1% named it the measure they were most interested in. UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies, polling September 15–20, found 31% yes and 40% no, with the rest undecided.
Governor Newsom, who took part in announcing the June deal, now opposes the measure. "This dangerous corporate power grab would let big corporations avoid paying their fair share and threaten billions in funding for critical services like 911 response and wildfire prevention. Vote NO on 43," he said in a statement the No campaign released (https://www.noprop43ca.com/news/statement-governor-newsom-announces-opposition-to-proposition-43) on October 9. Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for governor, announced his opposition on September 9. The California Democratic Party opposes (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 43, and the California Republican Party supports (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it.
The Voter Information Guide lists the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce in support, with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association as the Yes campaign's contact. Opponents listed in the No argument are the California Professional Firefighters, Californians Against Waste, the California Federation of Teachers, the California School Employees Association, Communities for a Better Environment, AAPI Force, the Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California, the Nurse Alliance of SEIU California and the Sierra Business Council. The Bay Area planning group SPUR recommends (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2026-11/ca-prop-43-local-tax-threshold) a no vote. The editorial boards we found have all recommended against it: the Santa Rosa Press Democrat (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/03/endorsement-prop-43-wants-to-fix-a-system-that-isnt-broken/) (October 3), the Santa Barbara Independent (https://www.independent.com/2026/10/07/the-santa-barbara-independent-endorsements-for-the-general-election-november-3-2026/) (October 7) and the Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316956235.html).
Proposition 43 after November 3 would mean a two-thirds rule from 2027 or no change to majority rule:
If Prop 43 passes, it takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State certifies the results, which is due December 11, and its two-thirds rule applies to voter-proposed special taxes approved from January 1, 2027. Measure ULA, Fresno's parks tax, San Francisco's Propositions C and G, and every other tax already approved would stay in force, but a renewal or increase of any of them would need two-thirds. Campaigns for new local taxes could still pass a general tax by majority. If it fails, the court-made rule stands: residents who gather signatures can pass a special tax with a simple majority, while councils and boards still need two-thirds. Either way, the broader Howard Jarvis initiative will not be on this ballot. It was withdrawn under the June deal.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, campaign-finance data as of October 14, 2026 (FPPC) and October 6, 2026 (Secretary of State), party positions as of October 12, 2026, and polling fielded through September 20, 2026.

Proposition 43 [Ballot] https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026 ### Translate Our Website Propositions on the November 3, 2026 Ballot November 3, 2026 ... # Proposition 43 ## Analysis of Measure ### Background Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors). Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them. A Bay Area lawmaker’s plea: Don’t vote for the state ballot measure she wrote
By Kathryn Palmer (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kathryn-palmer/) , Staff Writer July 3, 2026
Days after successfully placing a ballot measure on the November ballot, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks announced she is “adamantly opposed to it.”
Don Feria/For the S.F. Chronicle
Soon after 14 ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-ballot-measures-22319723.php) were locked in for California’s November election, the author of one of the propositions made an unusual declaration: She hopes no one votes for the measure she wrote.
Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, said on X this week that she wrote the measure “not because I wanted it to become law. But because it was the only path left to get the more dangerous initiative off the ballot before time ran out.”
Wicks’ Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22 is the kind of legislative compromise that has come to typify the ballot measure deadline process in recent years, using the Legislature’s ability to place measures on the ballot as a potential bargaining tool. Her plea for voters to reject the plan she created underscores the slapdash nature of the process at times — Wicks now says the eleventh-hour deal is better than nothing, but doesn’t actually want it to succeed.

A week earlier, on June 25, Wicks introduced the measure in the Assembly.
It was the final day for eligible citizen-led ballot initiatives to be pulled from the ballot before the November election, and Democratic lawmakers and interest groups were working frantically behind the scenes to find a legislative compromise to prevent a controversial tax measure from appearing on the ballot.
The measure, the Local Taxpayer Protection Act, would have had catastrophic consequences for local governments by severely limiting their ability to bring in new revenue by capping real estate transfer taxes and retroactively canceling any local tax increases that didn’t pass by a two-thirds margin — an extremely high bar that virtually no measures achieve.
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated in a July 2025 report (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) that the measure would have cost local governments “a couple of billion dollars” a year.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
After a series of false starts, Wicks’ new bill, ACA22 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22), persuaded the tax measure’s proponent, Jon Coupal of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, to nix the initiative. The Taxpayer Protection Act was withdrawn, ACA22 passed through both chambers, and the secretary of state’s office assigned it a name (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-ballot-measures-22319723.php): Proposition 43.
But just as soon as the saga around its last-minute approval ended, a new one emerged, signaling the start of what will probably be a costly and bruising campaign over the tax proposition, despite its genesis as a compromise between opposing groups.
The compromise offered a slimmed-down version of the original measure, sidestepping any caps on real estate transfer taxes and nixing the retroactive cancellation of voter-approved tax measures. But it still proposes that any new local taxes earmarked for specific purposes pass with a two-thirds vote, rather than a simple majority.
“People do use the initiative power as a way to negotiate, and this is a first for us,” Coupal said. “We initially thought we would be going to voters with the first initiative, but the way this worked out, this is better for us. It’s much cleaner and deals with a single issue.”
While Coupal has applauded the deal, Wicks and aligned interest groups characterize it as less bad, but still deeply unpalatable.

“ It would have essentially outlawed transfer taxes writ large — that’s why this was like a nuclear bomb, essentially,” Wicks said. “So we were trying to minimize that as much as possible. What we ended up with was this more narrow version of a bad initiative.”
Affordable housing advocates, including the prominent pro-housing nonprofit California YIMBY and the Housing Action Coalition, have long criticized high transfer taxes as obstacles to building more housing in the state.
In a statement posted to YIMBY’s website the day after the June 25 deadline, group President Brian Hanlon wrote outright, “We failed,” bemoaning ACA22 and the failure to pass an earlier compromise bill, AB736, which would have addressed real estate transfer taxes.
Shane Phillips, housing initiative manager at UCLA’s Lewis Center for Regional Policy Studies, said transfer taxes can be thought of as one-time service fees.
They are one-time levies applied to property sales. California has had these taxes for decades, Phillips said, but over the past several years more than a dozen cities have implemented their own, additional transfer tax rates. San Francisco voters approved Proposition I in 2020, increasing taxes on high-value real estate sales in the multimillions.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
These higher rates can disincentivize property sales, said Phillips, who has argued for a more progressive transfer tax system to tackle the issue. Sellers will either hold on to the property longer, Phillips said, or drive up the price of a sale in anticipation of the transfer tax bill later down the line. It’s a similar argument among pro-housing groups (https://cayimby.org/legislation/ab-736/), which say the increased rates have negatively impacted local housing production.
“I think what’s interested people in this is these unintended consequences,” Phillips said. “Reductions in (property) transactions reduce property tax growth, and that’s going to impact everyone if it cannibalizes tax revenues.”
In June, San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie and Supervisor Bilal Mahmood dropped their own controversial proposal, the BUILD Act, that would have cut transfer taxes on high-end real estate transactions.
It would have decreased transfer tax to pre-2020 levels, from 5.75% to 2.75% for transactions of at least $10 million and from 6% to 3% for deals of at least $25 million.
Transfer taxes brought $324 million to the city from 2021 to 2024, the Chronicle reported (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/mayor-lurie-drops-transfer-tax-plan-housing-22299548.php), and are a significant revenue source for cities across the state.

Article continues below this ad
With the deal, Coupal said, the issue of transfer tax caps is deferred “for the time being,” leaving the door open for future fights over what has become a flash point among developers, housing advocates and YIMBY-aligned groups.
“We were surprised the deal came together. We are pleased it did, because we like the outcome,” Coupal said.
In the Bay Area, Prop 43’s heightened vote threshold would make it harder for future local tax measures to pass. If passed, measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 Measure B funding healthcare, Sonoma County’s 2024 Measure H for fire protection and Santa Clara’s June 2026 Measure D for open space preservation would not have made it to the finish line — all received less than a two-thirds vote.
While Proposition 43 doesn’t tackle the transfer tax, it still risks confusing voters, Wicks said, pointing to that possibility as the reason why she wrote about her opposition to it on social media.
“It’s going to be a long and complicated ballot,” Wicks said. “It’s going to require folks really sit down at their kitchen table with their pamphlet and Google and do a lot of research on all these different measures. There’s going to be a lot of money coming at them from all sides, and it’s going to be a big tax fight on the ballot this cycle.”

content.text:
I'm not going to pick a side for you on this one. I read the measure, the Legislative Analyst's report, the ballot arguments, polls, campaign filings and editorials from both sides. Both sides agree on what the measure does. The disagreement is over priorities, which I don't know, so a bare yes or no from me would be a guess. On a contested ballot measure I'd rather inform your decision than make it.

**Your one-word answer, depending on your view**
- **Yes** if an earmarked local tax should need two-thirds approval whether a city council or a petition drive puts it on the ballot. That means a bit over one-third of voters could block a tax most voters want.
- **No** if a simple majority should be enough when residents qualify a tax by petition. That means some earmarked taxes would pass with less than two-thirds support.

Tell me which sounds more like you, and I'll give you the one word.

**What Prop 43 does and doesn't do**
- **New rule:** From Jan. 1, 2027, new, increased or extended *special* (earmarked) local taxes proposed by citizen initiative would need 66.7% instead of 50%+1.
- **Unchanged:**
  - General (unearmarked) taxes still need only a majority.
  - Earmarked taxes proposed by councils or boards already need two-thirds.
  - Existing taxes stay in place, though renewals or increases would need two-thirds.
  - Every local measure on this year's ballot is decided under the current rule.
- **Transfer taxes:** There is no cap on real-estate transfer taxes. That was in a broader Howard Jarvis initiative, withdrawn in a June 25 deal, and Prop 43 is the narrower replacement.
- **Property tax clause:** A second clause extends the existing 1% property-tax limit to initiatives. Its practical effect is unclear.
- **Permanence and revenue:** It's a constitutional amendment, so only another statewide vote could undo it. The Legislative Analyst says local revenue "could be lower" by an "unknown" amount.
- **Thresholds matter:** When school-bond approval dropped from two-thirds to 55% in 2000, passage rates rose nearly 30%.

**The real dispute**

The question is whether citizen initiatives are a legitimate way for communities to tax themselves, or a loophole.
- **Supporters** say officials and allied groups are closely involved in what are formally "citizens'" initiatives, such as the Bay Area's Measure RTM and L.A. County's Measure A.
- **Opponents** point to measures that would have failed, such as Sonoma County's fire and emergency sales tax (about 62%) and L.A.'s Measure ULA (58%).
- CalMatters reports more than two dozen such taxes have passed under the majority rule since 2017.

**Where each side stretches**
- **Yes:**
  - The "2,000 new taxes" figure and the transfer-tax examples aren't what Prop 43 changes.
  - I found no new "spend it as promised" rule in the text.
  - The "nearly unanimous" legislative vote (68–2 and 35–1) was a deal to avoid a worse initiative. Its author, Buffy Wicks, Gov. Newsom and the state Democratic Party now oppose it.
- **No:**
  - The "$3 billion a year" figure is the campaign's own hypothetical, not a Legislative Analyst number.
  - Earmarked fire and police taxes proposed by local governments already need two-thirds.
  - The "one-third can block two-thirds" point is accurate.
- **Money:** The Yes side's funding is mostly the California Business Roundtable PAC and real-estate firms. The No side's is mostly labor unions.

**Where it stands**
- **Polls:** PPIC (Oct. 16–22) found 42% yes and 55% no. Berkeley IGS (Oct. 19–25) found 36% yes, 46% no and 18% undecided.
- **Supporting:** The Orange County Register, San Diego Union-Tribune, Mercury News and the Republican Party.
- **Opposing:** The Sacramento Bee, Santa Rosa Press Democrat, SPUR and the Democratic Party.
- **Neither:** The S.F. Chronicle said it wouldn't back or oppose it.

**Main sources:** [Official guide and LAO analysis](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/), [CalMatters on the deal](https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/), [CalMatters on the campaign](https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-prop-43-election-2026/), [Hoover "California Decides"](https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-43), [PPIC October poll](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), [Mercury News (yes)](https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/17/endorsement-back-prop-43-restore-voter-approved-restrictions-on-local-taxes-proposition-13/), [Sacramento Bee (no)](https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316956235.html).
